+---
+title: Switch between governed tenants (Preview)
+description: Learn how to find and switch to governed tenants in the Microsoft Entra admin center using existing delegated access.
+ms.topic: how-to
+ms.date: 11/11/2026
+ai-usage: ai-generated
+# Customer intent: As a delegated administrator, I want to find and switch to governed tenants without opening each governance relationship.
+---
+
+# Switch between governed tenants (Preview)
+
+The **Governed tenants** view in **Manage tenants** helps you find tenants you can administer through Microsoft Entra Tenant Governance. It uses active governance relationships and your active membership in their delegated-role groups.
+
+You can select a target without opening each governance relationship individually. Switching uses your existing access: it doesn't create a relationship, invite a guest, or grant additional permissions.
+
+## Prerequisites
+
+- Start with your member account in the governing tenant. Your home tenant is where this account originates, not whichever tenant the admin center currently displays.
+- Have an active direct governance relationship with the target tenant and active membership in a group referenced by its delegated role assignments.
+- Have the delegated role required for the task you want to perform in the target tenant.
+
+If your group membership is eligible through Privileged Identity Management (PIM), activate it before using the governed-tenant discovery view. Eligible membership alone doesn't qualify. See [Use cross-tenant delegated administration](how-to-delegated-administration.md).
+
+## Find your governed tenants
+
+Use the discovery view to identify the tenant you intend to administer.
+
+1. Sign in to the [Microsoft Entra admin center](https://entra.microsoft.com) using your governing-tenant member account.
+1. Browse to **Entra ID** > **Overview** > **Manage tenants**.
+1. Select **Governed tenants**.
+1. Find the target tenant and verify its **Organization ID**.
+
+The list reflects qualifying active relationships and group membership. A terminated relationship doesn't contribute access. A tenant can remain listed if another active relationship still qualifies your account.
+
+Use the existing directory list for ordinary tenant membership and B2B guest access. A B2B invitation alone doesn't place a tenant in **Governed tenants**.
+
+## Switch to a governed tenant
+
+Check the target identity before switching or making administrative changes.
+
+1. In **Governed tenants**, compare the target's **Organization ID** with the tenant you intend to administer.
+1. Select **Switch** for that tenant.
+1. Complete any sign-in prompts.
+1. Verify the tenant identity in the admin center before performing administrative tasks.
+
+> [!IMPORTANT]
+> A discovery result isn't a guarantee that every sign-in or operation will succeed. Target permissions and sign-in requirements still apply. Your actions remain limited to the access already granted.
+
+Don't rely on a display name or a domain-name column as the only identity check.
+
+## Return to your home tenant
+
+You can return to your home tenant to choose another governed tenant.
+
+1. In the governed tenant, open **Entra ID** > **Overview** > **Manage tenants**.
+1. Select **View home tenant**.
+1. Verify that the admin center is in your home tenant, open **Governed tenants**, and select the next target.
+
+## Understand the access boundary
+
+Multi-tier relationships don't add indirect targets. If A governs B and B governs C, a user in A doesn't gain access to C through that chain. A needs a separately approved direct relationship with C and the user needs qualifying group membership.
+
+The **Governed tenants** view isn't a combined inventory of every B2B, CSP, or Partner Center relationship. It reflects access through Tenant Governance.
+
+## Troubleshooting
+
+| Issue | What to check |
+| --- | --- |
+| **Governed tenants** isn't available | Verify the account and tenant context and the availability of the preview in your environment. Don't assign Global Administrator solely to reveal the view. |
+| The list is empty or a target is missing | Check the active direct relationship, active group membership, and current tenant context. Clear filters, refresh, or sign in again after access changes. |
+| The tenant is listed but switching fails | Ask the target administrator to review delegated grants and sign-in requirements. |
+| Access was recently removed | Refresh or sign in again after changes propagate. Check whether another active relationship still grants access. |
+| Tenant names are similar or details appear unexpected | Verify the **Organization ID** and actual assigned permissions before making changes. |
+
+For support, record the current tenant, target tenant ID, account context, failing step, UTC time, and error or correlation ID. Don't share access tokens, cookies, or credentials.
+
+## Related content
+
+- [Use cross-tenant delegated administration](how-to-delegated-administration.md).
+- [Governance relationships](governance-relationships.md).
+- [Set up multi-tier governance relationships](how-to-set-up-multi-tier-governance.md).
+- [Monitor governing tenant activity](how-to-monitor-governing-activity.md).

They differ in retention, initial difference-report and recovery performance, licensing, and billing. + +Identity administrators can use this comparison to choose the plan that meets their organization's retention and billing needs. + +> [!NOTE] +> The Premium plan is in preview and must be turned on in the Microsoft 365 admin center. To get started, see [Set up Microsoft 365 Backup](/microsoft-365/backup/backup-setup?view=o365-worldwide). + + + +## Compare Standard and Premium plans + +The following table summarizes the plan differences. + +| **Capability** | **Standard plan** | **Premium plan (preview)** | +| --- | --- | --- | +| **Retention** | Up to 7 days of daily backups. | Up to 30 days of daily backups. | +| **Backup frequency** | Once a day. | Once a day. | +| **[Supported objects](scope-supported-objects-limitations.md)** | All object types supported by Microsoft Entra Backup and Recovery. | The same supported object types as the Standard plan. | +| **Difference reports and recovery** | The first operation against an unloaded backup loads the backup data. Later operations against the same backup reuse the loaded data. | Initial processing skips data loading, allowing faster full difference-report generation or recovery. | +| **Recovery scope** | Recover all supported objects, selected object types, or specific object IDs. | The same recovery scope as the Standard plan. | +| **Licensing prerequisites** | Included with Microsoft Entra ID P1 and P2 licenses. | Microsoft Entra ID P1 and P2 licenses aren't required. The tenant must have at least one SharePoint license or a license that includes SharePoint. | +| **Billing model** | Included with Microsoft Entra ID P1 and P2 licenses. | Consumption-based billing at $0.025 USD per protected object per month. For pricing details, see [Microsoft Entra Backup and Recovery Premium pricing](backup-recovery-premium-pricing.md). | +| **Default state** | Available automatically for tenants with Microsoft Entra ID P1 or P2 licenses. | Off by default. | + +## How Premium retention accumulates + +Premium backup history grows after each daily backup cycle until 30 days are available. + +For a tenant that already has Standard plan backups: + +| **Time after Premium is enabled** | **Available backup history** | **Premium billing** | +| --- | --- | --- | +| **Day 1** | Six Standard backups and one Premium backup. | One day of Premium backup data. | +| **Day 2** | Five Standard backups and two Premium backups. | Two days of Premium backup data. | +| **Day 30** | Thirty Premium backups in a rolling window. | Thirty days of Premium backup data. | + +For a tenant without Microsoft Entra ID P1 or P2 licenses, backup history starts with the first Premium backup and grows by one backup after each daily backup cycle. + +## How to identify the plan type + +To identify your tenant's current plan, go to **Backup and recovery** > **Settings** in the Microsoft Entra admin center. Under **Plan status**, **Current plan** shows **Standard** or **Premium**. + +:::image type="content" source="media/backup-recovery-plans/plan-status.png" alt-text="Screenshot of the Backup and recovery Settings page showing Premium as the current plan under Plan status." lightbox="media/backup-recovery-plans/plan-status.png"::: + +To identify the plan associated with a specific backup, go to **Backups** and check the **Plan** column. Each backup shows **Standard** or **Premium**. Retained Standard and Premium backups can appear together and are sorted by date. + +:::image type="content" source="media/backup-recovery-plans/backup-plan-column.png" alt-text="Screenshot of the Backups page showing Standard and Premium values in the Plan column." lightbox="media/backup-recovery-plans/backup-plan-column.png"::: + +## What happens when Premium stops + +Premium can stop because an administrator turns it off or because of a billing issue. In either case: + +- The service stops creating new Premium backups. +- Existing Premium backups remain available for difference reports and recovery jobs until they expire. +- The **Plan** column continues to identify retained Premium backups. + +For tenants with Microsoft Entra ID P1 or P2 licenses, new Standard backups begin accumulating after Premium stops. The backup list can contain retained Premium backups and new Standard backups at the same time. + +For tenants without Microsoft Entra ID P1 or P2 licenses, no new Standard backups are created. + +If Premium stops because of a billing issue, use the Microsoft 365 admin center to review the billing status. + +## Related content + +- [Microsoft Entra Backup and Recovery Premium pricing](backup-recovery-premium-pricing.md) +- [Microsoft Entra Backup and Recovery overview](overview.md) +- [View available backups](view-available-backups.md) +- [Supported objects and recoverable properties](scope-supported-objects-limitations.md)

@@ -0,0 +1,52 @@
+---
+title: Microsoft Entra Backup and Recovery Premium pricing (preview)
+description: Learn how Microsoft Entra Backup and Recovery Premium pricing works and estimate monthly costs based on the number of protected objects.
+author: tazkiaafra
+ms.author: tazkiaafra
+ms.date: 11/16/2026
+ms.service: entra-id
+ms.topic: concept-article
+ms.custom: msecd-doc-authoring-1026
+ai-usage: ai-generated
+
+#customer intent: As an identity administrator, I want to estimate Microsoft Entra Backup and Recovery Premium costs so that I can plan my organization's backup budget.
+---
+
+# Microsoft Entra Backup and Recovery Premium pricing (preview)
+
+Microsoft Entra Backup and Recovery Premium uses consumption-based pricing. The price is $0.025 USD per protected Microsoft Entra object per month.
+
+Use the pricing formula and example in this article to estimate your monthly cost. The estimate helps with planning, but your actual charges depend on billed usage.
+
+> [!NOTE]
+> The Premium plan is in preview and must be turned on in the Microsoft 365 admin center. To get started, see [Set up Microsoft 365 Backup](/microsoft-365/backup/backup-setup?view=o365-worldwide).
+
+## Pricing model
+
+Estimate the monthly cost by multiplying the number of protected Microsoft Entra objects by the monthly price per object:
+
+`Estimated monthly cost = number of protected objects × $0.025 USD`
+
+The estimate uses the number of protected objects as its input.
+
+## Pricing example
+
+The following examples estimate the cost for a full month when the protected-object count remains constant.
+
+| Protected objects | Calculation | Estimated monthly cost |
+| --- | --- | ---: |
+| **10,000** | 10,000 × $0.025 USD | $250 USD |
+| **50,000** | 50,000 × $0.025 USD | $1,250 USD |
+| **100,000** | 100,000 × $0.025 USD | $2,500 USD |
+| **500,000** | 500,000 × $0.025 USD | $12,500 USD |
+| **1,000,000** | 1,000,000 × $0.025 USD | $25,000 USD |
+
+## Billing through Microsoft 365 Backup
+
+Billing for Premium is processed through Microsoft 365 Backup. For commerce billing, protected-object usage is represented as GB-based billing units. These units don't indicate the amount of backup storage consumed. For details, see the [Microsoft 365 Backup pricing model](/microsoft-365/backup/backup-pricing?view=o365-worldwide).
+
+## Related content
+
+- [Compare Standard and Premium plans](backup-recovery-plans.md)
+- [Microsoft Entra Backup and Recovery overview](overview.md)
+- [Pricing model for Microsoft 365 Backup](/microsoft-365/backup/backup-pricing?view=o365-worldwide)

diff --git a/docs/agent-id/agent-authorization-code-oauth-flow.md b/docs/agent-id/agent-authorization-code-oauth-flow.md
new file mode 100644
index 00000000000..bd5bb6e7edb
--- /dev/null
+++ b/docs/agent-id/agent-authorization-code-oauth-flow.md
@@ -0,0 +1,145 @@
+---
+title: OAuth 2.0 authorization code grant
+description: Learn how public and confidential clients use the authorization code grant with Agent ID.
+titleSuffix: Microsoft Entra Agent ID
+ms.topic: reference
+ms.date: 11/05/2026
+ai-usage: ai-assisted
+ms.reviewer: jmprieur
+
+#customer-intent: As a developer, I want to understand how public and confidential clients use the authorization code grant in an Agent ID solution.
+---
+
+# OAuth 2.0 authorization code grant
+
+The OAuth 2.0 authorization code grant signs in a user and obtains tokens with delegated permissions. The user signs in through a browser, Microsoft Entra ID returns a short-lived authorization code, and the client redeems the code at the token endpoint.
+
+An Agent ID solution can use the grant in two ways:
+
+| Client type | Typical role | Client credential | PKCE |
+| --- | --- | --- | --- |
+| Public client | A local agent signs in the user directly. | No | Required |
+| Confidential client | A server-side web client signs in the user before calling a hosted agent. | Yes | Recommended |
+
+Use Microsoft Authentication Library (MSAL) or Microsoft.Identity.Web instead of creating these requests directly. The requests in this article show the protocol fields for reference.
+
+[!INCLUDE [Use Microsoft SDKs](./includes/use-microsoft-libraries.md)]
+
+> [!IMPORTANT]
+> Public-client Agent ID support is in preview. This preview is provided without a service-level agreement and isn't recommended for production workloads. Some features might be unsupported or have constrained capabilities. For more information, see [Universal License Terms for Online Services](https://www.microsoft.com/licensing/terms/product/ForOnlineServices/all).
+
+## Authorization request
+
+Both client types send the user to the tenant's authorization endpoint:
+
+```http
+GET https://login.microsoftonline.com/{tenant-id}/oauth2/v2.0/authorize?
+    client_id={client-id}
+    &response_type=code
+    &redirect_uri={encoded-redirect-uri}
+    &response_mode=query
+    &scope=openid%20profile%20offline_access%20api://{resource-client-id}/{scope}
+    &state={random-state}
+    &nonce={random-nonce}
+    &code_challenge={pkce-challenge}
+    &code_challenge_method=S256
+```
+
+- `client_id` identifies the public or confidential client. A CIMD-based public client uses its HTTPS metadata document URL as the client ID.
+- `redirect_uri` must exactly match a redirect URI configured for the client.
+- `scope` contains the delegated permissions the client requests. Omit the resource scope when the client only needs to sign in the user.
+- `state` binds the response to the initiating session and helps prevent cross-site request forgery.
+- `nonce` binds an OpenID Connect ID token to the initiating session.
+- `code_challenge` is derived from a high-entropy PKCE verifier by using SHA-256.
+
+After sign-in and consent, Microsoft Entra ID redirects the browser to the registered redirect URI:
+
+```http
+GET {redirect-uri}?code={authorization-code}&state={state}
+```
+
+Before redeeming the code, validate `state` and handle any OAuth error returned to the redirect URI.
+
+## Public client token request
+
+A public client can't protect a client credential. It redeems the code by using the PKCE verifier:
+
+```http
+POST https://login.microsoftonline.com/{tenant-id}/oauth2/v2.0/token
+Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
+
+client_id={agent-id-client-id-or-cimd-url}
+&grant_type=authorization_code
+&code={authorization-code}
+&redirect_uri={redirect-uri}
+&scope=openid profile offline_access api://{resource-client-id}/{scope}
+&code_verifier={pkce-verifier}
+```
+
+Don't send a client secret, certificate assertion, or federated credential in this request.
+
+A registered public-client Agent ID must use [single-instance mode](agent-blueprint.md#instance-modes-preview). A client that uses a [Client ID Metadata Document](client-id-metadata-documents.md) can use the document's HTTPS URL as its client ID. For implementation guidance, see [Sign in users from a local agent](authenticate-local-agent.md).
+
+## Confidential client token request
+
+A confidential client runs on a server that can protect credentials. The server, not browser code, redeems the authorization code. The request includes a client credential and the PKCE verifier when the authorization request used PKCE:
+
+```http
+POST https://login.microsoftonline.com/{tenant-id}/oauth2/v2.0/token
+Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
+
+client_id={confidential-client-id}
+&grant_type=authorization_code
+&code={authorization-code}
+&redirect_uri={redirect-uri}
+&scope=openid profile offline_access api://{agent-blueprint-client-id}/{scope}
+&code_verifier={pkce-verifier}
+&client_assertion_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:client-assertion-type:jwt-bearer
+&client_assertion={signed-client-assertion}
+```
+
+The example uses a certificate-based client assertion. A client secret is also supported, but use a certificate or workload identity federation when possible.
+
+In a hosted Agent ID solution, the confidential client is normally the upstream web application, not the child Agent ID. Request an access token whose audience is the hosted agent's blueprint, send that access token to the agent API, and use the [On-Behalf-Of flow](agent-on-behalf-of-oauth-flow.md) to call downstream APIs.
+
+For a single-instance agent identity (preview), `<agent-blueprint-client-id>` denotes the client ID shared by the blueprint and agent identity. For a fleet, it denotes the blueprint's client ID, not an individual child agent's ID. For single-instance mode, configure the upstream client's grant through [Grant the upstream client access](aspnet-core-authenticate-users.md#grant-the-upstream-client-access) before sign-in; browser consent doesn't support the agent identity as a resource.
+
+Don't send an authorization code or ID token to the hosted agent API. Child Agent IDs in the confidential-client pattern don't initiate an interactive `/authorize` request.
+
+## Token response
+
+If the request succeeds, Microsoft Entra ID returns tokens such as:
+
+```json
+{
+  "token_type": "Bearer",
+  "scope": "api://<resource-client-id>/<scope>",
+  "expires_in": 3599,
+  "access_token": "<access-token>",
+  "refresh_token": "<refresh-token>",
+  "id_token": "<id-token>"
+}
+```
+
+The exact response depends on the requested scopes:
+
+- Use the access token only with the resource identified by its `aud` claim.
+- Use the ID token to establish the user's sign-in session, not to call an API.
+- A refresh token is returned when the request and policy allow offline access.
+
+## Security requirements
+
+- Use PKCE with the `S256` challenge method for public clients. Also use PKCE for confidential clients when the library supports it.
+- Match the redirect URI exactly in the authorization and token requests.
+- Generate a new `state`, `nonce`, and PKCE verifier for each authorization request.
+- Redeem an authorization code only once and only from the client that started the request.
+- Don't log authorization codes, client credentials, access tokens, refresh tokens, or ID tokens.
+- Validate access tokens in the API. Don't treat possession of an authorization code or ID token as API authorization.
+
+## Related content
+
+- [Microsoft identity platform and OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow](/entra/identity-platform/v2-oauth2-auth-code-flow)
+- [Public client and confidential client applications](/entra/identity-platform/msal-client-applications)
+- [Redirect URI restrictions and limitations](/entra/identity-platform/reply-url)
+- [Certificate credentials for application authentication](/entra/identity-platform/certificate-credentials)
+- [Choose an authentication protocol for an agent](agent-oauth-protocols.md)

diff --git a/docs/agent-id/aspnet-core-authenticate-users.md b/docs/agent-id/aspnet-core-authenticate-users.md
new file mode 100644
index 00000000000..be19e32996f
--- /dev/null
+++ b/docs/agent-id/aspnet-core-authenticate-users.md
@@ -0,0 +1,232 @@
+---
+title: Authenticate users to an ASP.NET Core agent API
+description: Configure an ASP.NET Core agent API to validate access tokens obtained by an upstream client for signed-in users.
+titleSuffix: Microsoft Entra Agent ID
+ms.topic: how-to
+ms.date: 11/06/2026
+ai-usage: ai-assisted
+ms.reviewer: dastrock, jomondi
+#customer-intent: As a developer building a cloud agent, I want its ASP.NET Core API to validate user access tokens from an upstream client.
+---
+
+# Authenticate users to an ASP.NET Core agent API
+
+An upstream client signs in the user and sends an access token to your agent API. This article configures the ASP.NET Core agent API to validate that token and shows a local test client that signs in a user and calls `/whoami`.
+
+Authentication establishes the caller's identity. [Control user access to agents](control-user-access-agents.md) separately determines whether that identity can invoke the agent.
+
+## Prerequisites
+
+- Completion of [Create an identity for your agent](create-single-instance-agent.md), including the tenant enablement and administrator handoff. Record the shared client ID and the agent identity's object ID.
+- The [.NET 10 SDK](/dotnet/core/install/). The examples use Microsoft.Identity.Web 4.17.0.
+- An upstream client application that can sign in users and request an access token for the agent API, or permission to register the [local test client](#register-a-local-test-client).
+- For the preview consent step, the [management client](create-single-instance-agent.md#set-up-the-management-client) with administrator consent for the additional delegated Graph permission `DelegatedPermissionGrant.ReadWrite.All`. Use an administrator authorized to consent to these delegated permissions. Choose the least privileged supported role from [Grant tenant-wide admin consent](~/identity/enterprise-apps/grant-admin-consent.md), and confirm any additional preview consent requirements with your Microsoft representative.
+- A trusted local HTTPS development certificate for local testing. Run `dotnet dev-certs https --trust` and approve the trust prompt on your development machine. Don't disable certificate verification.
+
+## Register a local test client
+
+Skip this section if you already have a client that signs in users and calls your agent. This test client is a separate, ordinary app registration, not another agent identity.
+
+1. [Register a single-tenant application](~/identity-platform/quickstart-register-app.md) named **Agent API test client** in the agent's tenant.
+1. Under **Authentication**, add the **Mobile and desktop applications** platform with redirect URI `http://localhost`. No client secret is needed.
+1. Record its **Application (client) ID**. Under **Enterprise applications**, find the corresponding application and record its **Object ID**. Token requests use the client ID; consent grants use the enterprise application's object ID.
+
+The client uses a browser and PKCE. The loopback redirect receives the authorization response locally; API calls still use HTTPS.
+
+## Configure the delegated permission
+
+The upstream client needs a delegated permission to call the agent API for the signed-in user.
+
+1. On the blueprint, [expose an identifier URI and delegated scope](create-blueprint.md#configure-identifier-uri-and-scope). Use `access_agent` as the scope value for this walkthrough. Preserve existing scopes and set `api.requestedAccessTokenVersion` to `2`.
+1. Declare that scope in the upstream client's `requiredResourceAccess`. Use the shared agent client ID as `resourceAppId` and the exposed scope's GUID with `"type": "Scope"`.
+1. Grant the upstream client access for the test user as described in the next section. During preview, browser consent doesn't support an agent identity as the resource.
+
+For more information, see [Configure a client application to access a web API](~/identity-platform/quickstart-configure-app-access-web-apis.md) and [Permissions and consent in the Microsoft identity platform](~/identity-platform/permissions-consent-overview.md).
+
+Configure the upstream client by following the authentication flow for that client type. For example, see the [OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow](~/identity-platform/v2-oauth2-auth-code-flow.md). Request the fully qualified agent API scope:
+
+```text
+api://<agent-client-id>/access_agent
+```
+
+Use an authentication library in the upstream client. Don't send ID tokens or authorization codes to the agent API.
+
+## Grant the upstream client access
+
+Use the management client for these Microsoft Graph requests, not the agent's runtime credential. This grant authorizes the upstream client to call the agent; it doesn't grant the agent access to downstream APIs.
+
+Before running the requests, open the **management app's** registration in the Microsoft Entra admin center. Under **API permissions**, select **Add a permission** > **Microsoft Graph** > **Delegated permissions**, add `DelegatedPermissionGrant.ReadWrite.All`, and have an authorized administrator grant consent. Keep the two management permissions from provisioning. Don't add these permissions to the agent or the test client.
+
+Reconnect with all three consented scopes:
+
+```powershell
+Disconnect-MgGraph
+Connect-MgGraph -ClientId "<management-app-client-id>" `
+    -TenantId "<tenant-id>" `
+    -Scopes "AgentIdentityBlueprint.ReadWrite.All", "AgentIdentity.ReadWrite.All", "DelegatedPermissionGrant.ReadWrite.All" `
+    -ContextScope Process
+```
+
+Use `Invoke-MgGraphRequest` as shown in [Set up the management client](create-single-instance-agent.md#set-up-the-management-client).
+
+1. Check for an existing applicable grant:
+
+    ```http
+    GET https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/oauth2PermissionGrants?$filter=clientId eq '<upstream-client-service-principal-object-id>' and resourceId eq '<agent-identity-object-id>'
+    ```
+
+    Follow pagination. An applicable tenant-wide grant or a grant for the test user might already include `access_agent`.
+
+1. If no applicable grant exists, grant access for the one user who will sign in:
+
+    ```http
+    POST https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/oauth2PermissionGrants
+    Content-Type: application/json
+
+    {
+      "clientId": "<upstream-client-service-principal-object-id>",
+      "resourceId": "<agent-identity-object-id>",
+      "consentType": "Principal",
+      "principalId": "<user-object-id>",
+      "scope": "access_agent"
+    }
+    ```
+
+    `clientId` and `resourceId` are service principal **object IDs**, not OAuth client IDs. If a grant already exists for that user but lacks the scope, [update the OAuth2 permission grant scope](/graph/api/oauth2permissiongrant-update) with the union of existing and required scopes. Don't create a duplicate or remove unrelated scopes.
+
+1. Record the grant's `id` for cleanup. Sign in as that user when you [run the test client](#run-the-test-client). Don't force a new consent prompt against the agent resource.
+
+## Configure token validation
+
+Create the agent API project if you don't already have one:
+
+```dotnetcli
+dotnet new webapi --framework net10.0 --name AgentApi
+cd AgentApi
+```
+
+Install `Microsoft.Identity.Web` from the project directory:
+
+```dotnetcli
+dotnet add package Microsoft.Identity.Web --version 4.17.0
+```
+
+Configure the agent API in `appsettings.json`:
+
+```json
+{
+  "AzureAd": {
+    "Instance": "https://login.microsoftonline.com/",
+    "TenantId": "<tenant-id>",
+    "ClientId": "<agent-client-id>"
+  }
+}
+```
+
+Replace the project's `Program.cs` with the following code. It requires the `access_agent` scope before returning the caller's validated identity:
+
+```csharp
+using System.Security.Claims;
+using Microsoft.Identity.Web;
+using Microsoft.Identity.Web.Resource;
+
+var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);
+
+builder.Services.AddMicrosoftIdentityWebApiAuthentication(
+    builder.Configuration);
+builder.Services.AddAuthorization();
+
+var app = builder.Build();
+
+app.UseAuthentication();
+app.UseAuthorization();
+
+app.MapGet("/whoami", (HttpContext context) =>
+{
+    context.VerifyUserHasAnyAcceptedScope("access_agent");
+
+    ClaimsPrincipal user = context.User;
+    string? objectId = user.GetObjectId();
+    string? tenantId = user.GetTenantId();
+
+    return Results.Ok(new { objectId, tenantId });
+})
+.RequireAuthorization();
+
+app.Run();
+```
+
+`AddMicrosoftIdentityWebApiAuthentication` validates the token signature, issuer, audience, and lifetime. Authorization policies can then evaluate scopes, app roles, and other claims.
+
+`VerifyUserHasAnyAcceptedScope` rejects a valid token that doesn't contain the `access_agent` delegated permission.
+
+Use `GetObjectId()` and `GetTenantId()` to read the stable identity. These helpers handle both the original JWT claim names and the claim names mapped by the authentication middleware.
+
+## Understand the request path
+
+1. The upstream client signs in the user.
+1. The client obtains an access token for `access_agent`.
+1. The client sends `Authorization: Bearer <token>` to the agent API.
+1. The ASP.NET Core authentication middleware validates the token.
+1. The agent API applies its authorization policy.
+
+## Run the test client
+
+Start the agent API:
+
+```dotnetcli
+dotnet run --urls https://localhost:5001
+```
+
+In another terminal, create a console project outside the agent API directory:
+
+```dotnetcli
+dotnet new console --framework net10.0 --name AgentTestClient
+cd AgentTestClient
+dotnet add package Microsoft.Identity.Client
+```
+
+Replace the console project's `Program.cs` with this code. Substitute the tenant ID, test client's client ID, and agent's shared client ID:
+
+```csharp
+using System.Net.Http.Headers;
+using Microsoft.Identity.Client;
+
+var client = PublicClientApplicationBuilder.Create("<upstream-client-id>")
+    .WithAuthority("https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant-id>")
+    .WithRedirectUri("http://localhost")
+    .Build();
+
+var result = await client
+    .AcquireTokenInteractive(["api://<agent-client-id>/access_agent"])
+    .ExecuteAsync();
+
+using var http = new HttpClient();
+http.DefaultRequestHeaders.Authorization =
+    new AuthenticationHeaderValue("Bearer", result.AccessToken);
+using var response = await http.GetAsync("https://localhost:5001/whoami");
+Console.WriteLine($"HTTP {(int)response.StatusCode}");
+response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();
+Console.WriteLine(await response.Content.ReadAsStringAsync());
+```
+
+Run `dotnet run` and sign in as the user named in the consent grant. Expect `HTTP 200` and that user's object ID and tenant ID. A request to `/whoami` without a token must return `401`. Don't log the token or use an ID token in its place.
+
+If your API exposes another delegated scope and your test client has consent for it, also request a token for that scope alone and call `/whoami`. Confirm that the token has the agent API's audience but lacks `access_agent`, and that the request is rejected. This optional scope-negative test requires a second scope; the minimal local setup defines only `access_agent`. A token for a different audience tests audience validation, not scope authorization.
+
+If sign-in fails, check the test client's redirect URI and the per-user grant before changing the agent's configuration. If HTTPS fails, fix the development certificate's trust rather than bypassing validation.
+
+## Clean up the local test
+
+Stop both projects when you're done. Keep the test client and agent registration if you continue to the next task. When you no longer need a test grant, delete it with `DELETE https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/oauth2PermissionGrants/<grant-id>` through the management client, before deleting its client app registration. Don't delete shared clients or grants used by other users.
+
+## Next step
+
+[Call a custom API as the signed-in user](aspnet-core-call-custom-api-as-user.md). To restrict which users can invoke the agent, see [Control user access to agents](control-user-access-agents.md).
+
+## Related content
+
+- [Authenticate users to an agent fleet](aspnet-core-fleet-authenticate-users.md)
+- [Control user access to agents](control-user-access-agents.md)
+- [Request consent for delegated permissions](grant-agent-access-microsoft-365.md)
+- [Protected web API: verify scopes and app roles](/entra/identity-platform/scenario-protected-web-api-verification-scope-app-roles)

diff --git a/docs/agent-id/aspnet-core-call-azure-api-as-user.md b/docs/agent-id/aspnet-core-call-azure-api-as-user.md
new file mode 100644
index 00000000000..50477d57d29
--- /dev/null
+++ b/docs/agent-id/aspnet-core-call-azure-api-as-user.md
@@ -0,0 +1,137 @@
+---
+title: Call an Azure service as a user with ASP.NET Core
+description: Use an agent identity and the on-behalf-of flow to call an Azure service for the signed-in user.
+titleSuffix: Microsoft Entra Agent ID
+ms.topic: how-to
+ms.date: 11/05/2026
+ai-usage: ai-assisted
+ms.reviewer: dastrock, jomondi
+#customer-intent: As a developer building an interactive cloud agent, I want to call Azure services on behalf of the signed-in user.
+---
+
+# Call an Azure service as a user with ASP.NET Core
+
+Use the OAuth On-Behalf-Of (OBO) flow when an upstream client calls an agent API for a signed-in user and the agent calls an Azure service for that user.
+
+The agent API validates the access token from the upstream client. Microsoft.Identity.Web then uses ordinary confidential-client OBO to acquire an Azure access token for the signed-in user. The user's Azure role assignments determine which resources the downstream call can access.
+
+## Prerequisites
+
+- Complete [Authenticate users to an ASP.NET Core agent API](aspnet-core-authenticate-users.md).
+- A credential on the agent identity blueprint. For local testing, use the [registered certificate and local credential configuration](call-api-custom.md#configure-a-local-development-credential). Use a managed identity federated credential in production.
+- [User or administrator consent](grant-agent-access-microsoft-365.md) for the agent identity to use the Azure service's delegated scope.
+- An Azure RBAC role assigned to the signed-in user at the required scope.
+
+## Install the packages
+
+```dotnetcli
+dotnet add package Microsoft.Identity.Web
+```
+
+## Configure the blueprint credential
+
+Use the same `AzureAd` section that validates incoming tokens, and add the blueprint credential:
+
+The managed identity example requires an Azure host with that identity assigned and federation configured. On a workstation, use the local certificate configuration from the prerequisites instead; signing in to Azure CLI doesn't make the managed identity configuration work locally.
+
+```json
+{
+  "AzureAd": {
+    "Instance": "https://login.microsoftonline.com/",
+    "TenantId": "<tenant-id>",
+    "ClientId": "<agent-client-id>",
+    "ClientCredentials": [
+      {
+        "SourceType": "SignedAssertionFromManagedIdentity",
+        "ManagedIdentityClientId": "<managed-identity-client-id>"
+      }
+    ]
+  }
+}
+```
+
+[!INCLUDE [Dont use secrets](./includes/do-not-use-secrets.md)]
+
+## Configure token validation and OBO
+
+Replace the agent API's `Program.cs` from the authentication walkthrough with the following block, followed by the endpoint in **Call Azure Resource Manager**. Don't append a second application builder or `app.Run()`. This sample uses an in-memory token cache.
+
+```csharp
+using System.Net.Http.Headers;
+using Microsoft.Identity.Abstractions;
+using Microsoft.Identity.Web;
+using Microsoft.Identity.Web.Resource;
+
+var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);
+
+builder.Services
+    .AddMicrosoftIdentityWebApiAuthentication(builder.Configuration)
+    .EnableTokenAcquisitionToCallDownstreamApi()
+    .AddInMemoryTokenCaches();
+
+builder.Services.AddHttpClient();
+builder.Services.AddAuthorization();
+
+var app = builder.Build();
+
+app.UseAuthentication();
+app.UseAuthorization();
+```
+
+## Call Azure Resource Manager
+
+Use `CreateAuthorizationHeaderForUserAsync` with the authenticated `HttpContext.User`. The provider uses the agent's configured client ID and blueprint credential.
+
+The following endpoint enforces the agent API's `access_agent` scope, requests a delegated Azure Resource Manager token, and lists the subscriptions visible to the user:
+
+```csharp
+app.MapGet("/azure-subscriptions", async (
+    HttpContext context,
+    IAuthorizationHeaderProvider authorizationHeaderProvider,
+    IHttpClientFactory httpClientFactory) =>
+{
+    context.VerifyUserHasAnyAcceptedScope("access_agent");
+
+    string authorizationHeader = await authorizationHeaderProvider
+        .CreateAuthorizationHeaderForUserAsync(
+            ["https://management.azure.com/user_impersonation"],
+            claimsPrincipal: context.User);
+
+    HttpClient client = httpClientFactory.CreateClient();
+    client.DefaultRequestHeaders.Authorization =
+        AuthenticationHeaderValue.Parse(authorizationHeader);
+
+    using HttpResponseMessage response = await client.GetAsync(
+        "https://management.azure.com/subscriptions?api-version=2022-12-01");
+    response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();
+
+    return Results.Content(
+        await response.Content.ReadAsStringAsync(),
+        "application/json");
+})
+.RequireAuthorization();
+
+app.Run();
+```
+
+The returned authorization header includes the `Bearer` scheme. Send it only to the intended Azure service, and don't return or log it.
+
+For another Azure service, use the delegated scope, endpoint, and Azure RBAC role documented by that service.
+
+## Verify the Azure call
+
+1. Start the agent API with `dotnet run --urls https://localhost:5001` in the environment where its configured credential is available.
+1. In the [local test client](aspnet-core-authenticate-users.md#run-the-test-client), change the request URL to `https://localhost:5001/azure-subscriptions`. Keep the requested scope as `api://<agent-client-id>/access_agent`, not the Azure Resource Manager scope.
+1. Run the client and sign in as the user covered by both consent grants. Expect `HTTP 200` and a JSON subscription list. An empty list can be valid when the user has no visible subscriptions; compare it with the user's expected Azure access.
+1. Call the agent endpoint without a token and confirm `401 Unauthorized`.
+
+If token acquisition reports missing consent, check the agent identity's delegated Azure permission. If the Azure call is denied or expected subscriptions are absent, check the signed-in user's Azure RBAC assignments separately. The sample's `EnsureSuccessStatusCode` throws for a downstream failure; it doesn't forward that status to the client. Record correlation IDs and request times, not tokens.
+
+Stop the API and test client when you're done. Follow the steps to [clean up the local agent authentication test](aspnet-core-authenticate-users.md#clean-up-the-local-test), and remove only test-specific grants or Azure role assignments you created.
+
+## Related content
+
+- [Call a custom API as a user](aspnet-core-call-custom-api-as-user.md)
+- [Azure Resource Manager REST API](/rest/api/resources/)
+- [Azure built-in roles](/azure/role-based-access-control/built-in-roles)
+- [Call an Azure service as an agent](call-api-azure-services.md)

@@ -0,0 +1,235 @@
+---
+title: Call a custom API as a user with ASP.NET Core
+description: Call a custom API for a signed-in user from an ASP.NET Core agent.
+titleSuffix: Microsoft Entra Agent ID
+ms.topic: how-to
+ms.date: 11/06/2026
+ms.reviewer: dastrock, jomondi
+ai-usage: ai-assisted
+ms.custom: msecd-doc-authoring-1013
+#customer-intent: As a developer building an interactive cloud agent, I want to call my protected API on behalf of the signed-in user.
+---
+
+# Call a custom API as a user with ASP.NET Core
+
+Call your custom API with the signed-in user's access, rather than the agent's application permissions. This article uses the OAuth On-Behalf-Of (OBO) flow: a client signs in the user, calls your agent, and the agent gets a token for the downstream API.
+
+You'll extend the agent API from the authentication walkthrough and test the complete call with the same client. You can use an existing protected API or the local test API below. The agent doesn't start another interactive sign-in.
+
+## Prerequisites
+
+- Complete [Authenticate users to an ASP.NET Core agent API](aspnet-core-authenticate-users.md).
+- A credential on the agent identity blueprint. For local testing, use the [certificate registered during provisioning](create-single-instance-agent.md#add-a-certificate-for-confidential-clients) and the [local certificate configuration](call-api-custom.md#configure-a-local-development-credential). For production, configure a [managed identity federated credential](create-blueprint.md#configure-credentials-for-the-agent-identity-blueprint).
+- An existing custom API's delegated scope, HTTPS endpoint, and user authorization requirements, or permission to [set up the local test API](#prepare-a-downstream-api).
+- The management client and consent permissions from the authentication walkthrough, to grant the test user's downstream access.
+- An app role assigned to the user if the agent uses [app roles to control access](control-user-access-agents.md).
+
+The authentication walkthrough establishes client-to-agent consent. You also need agent-to-API consent; one grant doesn't replace the other.
+
+## Prepare a downstream API
+
+For an existing API, ask its owner for the application (client) ID, enterprise application object ID, fully qualified delegated scope, HTTPS endpoint, and test user's access requirements. Skip the local API steps only when that API is ready to validate and authorize delegated requests.
+
+To create an isolated local API:
+
+1. [Register a single-tenant application](~/identity-platform/quickstart-register-app.md) named **Agent downstream test API**.
+1. [Expose a delegated permission](~/identity-platform/quickstart-configure-app-expose-web-apis.md) with application ID URI `api://<custom-api-client-id>` and scope value `read_data`. Record the scope's GUID. In the app manifest, set `api.requestedAccessTokenVersion` to `2`.
+1. Record the corresponding enterprise application's **Object ID** for consent. Don't use its client ID in place of this object ID.
+1. Create a web API project in a separate directory:
+
+    ```dotnetcli
+    dotnet new webapi --framework net10.0 --name DownstreamApi
+    cd DownstreamApi
+    dotnet add package Microsoft.Identity.Web --version 4.17.0
+    ```
+
+1. Configure `AzureAd` in this project's `appsettings.json` with `Instance` set to `https://login.microsoftonline.com/`, your `TenantId`, and `ClientId` set to the **downstream API's** client ID. This resource API validates tokens and doesn't need a client credential.
+1. Replace this project's `Program.cs` with:
+
+    ```csharp
+    using Microsoft.Identity.Web;
+    using Microsoft.Identity.Web.Resource;
+
+    var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);
+    builder.Services.AddMicrosoftIdentityWebApiAuthentication(builder.Configuration);
+    builder.Services.AddAuthorization();
+    var app = builder.Build();
+    app.UseAuthentication();
+    app.UseAuthorization();
+
+    app.MapGet("/user-data", (HttpContext context) =>
+    {
+        context.VerifyUserHasAnyAcceptedScope("read_data");
+        return Results.Ok(new
+        {
+            objectId = context.User.GetObjectId(),
+            tenantId = context.User.GetTenantId()
+        });
+    }).RequireAuthorization();
+
+    app.Run();
+    ```
+
+1. Run `dotnet run --urls https://localhost:5002` and leave this terminal open. Use the trusted development certificate from the authentication walkthrough.
+
+The test endpoint returns only the authenticated caller's identity. For real data, enforce the user's access to each requested resource as well as the delegated scope. A scope alone doesn't authorize access to another user's records.
+
+## Grant downstream access
+
+Declare the API's delegated scope on the blueprint using [Declare the API permissions](create-single-instance-agent.md#declare-the-api-permissions). Use the downstream API's client ID for `resourceAppId` and its scope GUID with `"type": "Scope"`. A declaration isn't consent.
+
+Through the authorized management client, check for an existing grant:
+
+```http
+GET https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/oauth2PermissionGrants?$filter=clientId eq '<agent-identity-object-id>' and resourceId eq '<custom-api-service-principal-object-id>'
+```
+
+Follow pagination. If an applicable grant already includes the scope, reuse it. If a grant for this user lacks the scope, [update the OAuth2 permission grant](/graph/api/oauth2permissiongrant-update) with the union of existing and required scopes. Otherwise, grant access for the same user who signs in through the test client:
+
+```http
+POST https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/oauth2PermissionGrants
+Content-Type: application/json
+
+{
+  "clientId": "<agent-identity-object-id>",
+  "resourceId": "<custom-api-service-principal-object-id>",
+  "consentType": "Principal",
+  "principalId": "<user-object-id>",
+  "scope": "read_data"
+}
+```
+
+Expect `201 Created` and save the grant's `id` for cleanup. For an existing API, replace `read_data` with its scope value, without the `api://` prefix. For other consent options, see [Grant delegated permissions to an agent identity](grant-agent-access-microsoft-365.md).
+
+## Configure the blueprint credential
+
+Keep the agent API's existing `AzureAd` settings from the authentication walkthrough. Add the credential for where you run the API.
+
+# [Local workstation](#tab/local)
+
+Follow [Configure a local development credential](call-api-custom.md#configure-a-local-development-credential) to add the registered certificate in `appsettings.Development.json` and supply its password through the environment.
+
+Keep the tenant ID and agent client ID from the authentication walkthrough. Don't use the downstream API's client ID for the agent, and don't add a managed identity credential to the local configuration.
+
+# [Azure host](#tab/azure)
+
+Use the following `appsettings.json` configuration only on an Azure host with the specified managed identity assigned and its federated credential configured on the blueprint. Signing in to Azure CLI on your workstation doesn't make this configuration work locally.
+
+```json
+{
+  "AzureAd": {
+    "Instance": "https://login.microsoftonline.com/",
+    "TenantId": "<tenant-id>",
+    "ClientId": "<agent-client-id>",
+    "ClientCredentials": [
+      {
+        "SourceType": "SignedAssertionFromManagedIdentity",
+        "ManagedIdentityClientId": "<managed-identity-client-id>"
+      }
+    ]
+  }
+}
+```
+
+---
+
+[!INCLUDE [Dont use secrets](./includes/do-not-use-secrets.md)]
+
+## Configure token validation and OBO
+
+Replace the agent API's `Program.cs` from the authentication walkthrough with the following code and the endpoint in **Call the API**, in that order. Don't append a second application builder or a second `app.Run()`. This version adds token acquisition and uses an in-memory token cache for the local test.
+
+```csharp
+using System.Net.Http.Headers;
+using Microsoft.Identity.Abstractions;
+using Microsoft.Identity.Web;
+using Microsoft.Identity.Web.Resource;
+
+var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);
+
+builder.Services
+    .AddMicrosoftIdentityWebApiAuthentication(builder.Configuration)
+    .EnableTokenAcquisitionToCallDownstreamApi()
+    .AddInMemoryTokenCaches();
+
+builder.Services.AddHttpClient();
+builder.Services.AddAuthorization();
+
+var app = builder.Build();
+
+app.UseAuthentication();
+app.UseAuthorization();
+
+app.MapGet("/whoami", (HttpContext context) =>
+{
+    context.VerifyUserHasAnyAcceptedScope("access_agent");
+    return Results.Ok(new
+    {
+        objectId = context.User.GetObjectId(),
+        tenantId = context.User.GetTenantId()
+    });
+}).RequireAuthorization();
+```
+
+## Call the API
+
+Use `CreateAuthorizationHeaderForUserAsync` with the authenticated `HttpContext.User`. Microsoft.Identity.Web uses the validated incoming access token as the OBO assertion and authenticates with the configured shared client ID and blueprint credential.
+
+Append this endpoint after the `/whoami` mapping in the previous block. Keep `/whoami` so you can compare the inbound and downstream identities. Replace the client ID, scope value, and URL with your API's values. For the local test API, use `read_data` and `https://localhost:5002/user-data`.
+
+```csharp
+app.MapGet("/custom-api-for-user", async (
+    HttpContext context,
+    IAuthorizationHeaderProvider authorizationHeaderProvider,
+    IHttpClientFactory httpClientFactory) =>
+{
+    context.VerifyUserHasAnyAcceptedScope("access_agent");
+
+    string authorizationHeader = await authorizationHeaderProvider
+        .CreateAuthorizationHeaderForUserAsync(
+            ["api://<custom-api-client-id>/<delegated-scope>"],
+            claimsPrincipal: context.User);
+
+    HttpClient client = httpClientFactory.CreateClient();
+    client.DefaultRequestHeaders.Authorization =
+        AuthenticationHeaderValue.Parse(authorizationHeader);
+
+    using HttpResponseMessage response =
+        await client.GetAsync("https://api.contoso.com/user-data");
+    response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();
+
+    return Results.Content(
+        await response.Content.ReadAsStringAsync(),
+        response.Content.Headers.ContentType?.ToString());
+})
+.RequireAuthorization();
+
+app.Run();
+```
+
+The returned authorization header includes the `Bearer` scheme. Send it only to the intended custom API, and don't return or log it.
+
+The custom API must validate the token and enforce both the delegated scope and resource-level access for the user. For protocol details, see [OAuth protocols in Microsoft Entra Agent ID](agent-oauth-protocols.md#hosted-agent-that-acts-for-a-signed-in-user) and the [OAuth 2.0 On-Behalf-Of flow](/entra/identity-platform/v2-oauth2-on-behalf-of-flow).
+
+## Verify delegated access
+
+1. If the downstream API isn't already running, start it at `https://localhost:5002`. Leave it running while you start the agent API in its own terminal with `dotnet run --urls https://localhost:5001`.
+1. In the [test client](aspnet-core-authenticate-users.md#run-the-test-client), change only the request URL from `https://localhost:5001/whoami` to `https://localhost:5001/custom-api-for-user`. Keep the requested scope as `api://<agent-client-id>/access_agent`, not the downstream scope.
+1. Run the test client and sign in as the user in both consent grants. Expect `HTTP 200`. For the local API, the response must contain the same user and tenant IDs returned by `/whoami`.
+1. Call the agent endpoint without a bearer token. Expect `401`. A token issued for the agent must also be rejected if sent directly to the downstream API because its audience is wrong.
+1. For an existing API, test a resource the signed-in user isn't allowed to access. The local identity-only endpoint doesn't expose another user's records, so this resource-level test doesn't apply to it.
+
+If either API exposes another delegated scope, you can also run a scope-negative test against it. For a direct call from the test client, declare and grant that client the alternate scope on the target API. Request only that scope, then send the resulting token directly to that API's endpoint and confirm rejection. The token must have the target API's audience but lack the endpoint's required scope. If you instead test a downstream token acquired through OBO, the alternate downstream grant belongs to the agent identity, not the upstream test client. The minimal local setup doesn't define alternate scopes, so these tests are optional. Don't treat the wrong-audience test as a substitute.
+
+If OBO reports missing consent, check front-end access to the agent separately from the agent's downstream permission. OBO can't display an interactive consent prompt. Record correlation IDs for failures, not tokens or assertions.
+
+## Clean up the local test
+
+Stop the three projects. Through the management client, delete test-only grants with `DELETE https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/oauth2PermissionGrants/<grant-id>` before deleting their client or resource registrations. Delete the test client's and downstream API's app registrations only if you created them for this test. For a test-only agent, follow [Delete agent identity objects](howto-delete-agent-identity.md). Don't delete shared registrations, scopes, or grants.
+
+## Related content
+
+- [Call APIs for users of an agent fleet](aspnet-core-fleet-call-apis-as-user.md)
+- [Validate Agent ID tokens in a downstream API](how-to-validate-agent-tokens-downstream-api.md)
+- [Protected web API: verify scopes and app roles](/entra/identity-platform/scenario-protected-web-api-verification-scope-app-roles)
+- [Call a custom API as an agent](call-api-custom.md)

+++ b/docs/agent-id/aspnet-core-call-graph-as-user.md
@@ -0,0 +1,87 @@
+---
+title: Call Microsoft Graph as a user with ASP.NET Core
+description: Configure GraphServiceClient to call Microsoft Graph on behalf of a signed-in user through an agent identity.
+titleSuffix: Microsoft Entra Agent ID
+ms.topic: how-to
+ms.date: 11/05/2026
+ai-usage: ai-assisted
+ms.reviewer: dastrock, jomondi
+#customer-intent: As a developer building an interactive cloud agent, I want to call Microsoft Graph on behalf of the signed-in user.
+---
+
+# Call Microsoft Graph as a user with ASP.NET Core
+
+Use Microsoft Graph to read the signed-in user's profile through your agent API.
+
+In this article, the client calls the agent with an agent API token. Microsoft.Identity.Web exchanges it for a delegated Graph token without starting another interactive sign-in.
+
+## Prerequisites
+
+- Complete [Authenticate users to an ASP.NET Core agent API](aspnet-core-authenticate-users.md), including the local test client.
+- Reuse the [blueprint credential and OBO services](aspnet-core-call-custom-api-as-user.md#configure-the-blueprint-credential). You don't need that walkthrough's custom downstream API registration, consent grant, or local API project for this Graph example.
+- Declare the Microsoft Graph delegated permission `User.Read` on the blueprint and [grant delegated Microsoft Graph permissions to the agent identity](grant-agent-access-microsoft-365.md) for the test user. Client-to-agent consent doesn't grant the agent access to Graph.
+
+## Add Microsoft Graph
+
+Install the integration package:
+
+```dotnetcli
+dotnet add package Microsoft.Identity.Web.GraphServiceClient
+```
+
+Register `GraphServiceClient` with the services configured in the parent article. For this example, call `builder.Services.AddMicrosoftGraph` with `options.BaseUrl` set to `https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0` and `options.Scopes` set to `["User.Read"]`. This configures downstream Graph access, not the incoming agent API's permission.
+
+Place this registration before `builder.Build()` in the agent API's `Program.cs`.
+
+```csharp
+builder.Services.AddMicrosoftGraph(options =>
+{
+    options.BaseUrl = "https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0";
+    options.Scopes = ["User.Read"];
+});
+```
+
+## Call Microsoft Graph
+
+`GraphServiceClient` uses the authenticated user assertion from the request and the configured shared client ID. Don't set `RequestAppToken` or an Agent ID override; this call uses ordinary delegated access.
+
+Require authentication and verify the incoming `access_agent` scope before calling `graphClient.Me.GetAsync()`. The incoming token is for the agent API; Microsoft.Identity.Web acquires a different token for Microsoft Graph.
+
+Merge the following `using` directives with those at the top of `Program.cs`, and place the endpoint before its single `app.Run()`. You can omit the custom API endpoint from the parent walkthrough.
+
+```csharp
+using Microsoft.Graph;
+using Microsoft.Identity.Web;
+using Microsoft.Identity.Web.Resource;
+
+app.MapGet("/graph-me", async (
+    HttpContext context,
+    GraphServiceClient graphClient) =>
+{
+    context.VerifyUserHasAnyAcceptedScope("access_agent");
+
+    var user = await graphClient.Me.GetAsync();
+
+    return Results.Ok(new
+    {
+        user?.Id,
+        user?.DisplayName,
+        user?.UserPrincipalName
+    });
+})
+.RequireAuthorization();
+```
+
+The example requires `User.Read`. Add only the delegated permissions required by your Graph calls.
+
+## Verify the Graph call
+
+Start the agent API with `dotnet run --urls https://localhost:5001`. In the [local test client](aspnet-core-authenticate-users.md#run-the-test-client), change only the request URL to `https://localhost:5001/graph-me`; keep the agent API scope. Sign in as the user covered by both grants. Expect `HTTP 200` and that user's profile, with `id` matching the object ID returned by `/whoami`.
+
+A call without a token must return `401`. If token acquisition reports missing consent, check the agent-to-Graph grant separately from the client's access to the agent. OBO can't display an interactive consent prompt. Stop the projects when finished and follow the steps to [clean up the local agent authentication test](aspnet-core-authenticate-users.md#clean-up-the-local-test) for test-only resources.
+
+## Related content
+
+- [Call a custom API as a user](aspnet-core-call-custom-api-as-user.md)
+- [Microsoft Graph permissions reference](/graph/permissions-reference)
+- [Call Microsoft Graph as an agent](call-api-microsoft-graph.md)

+---
+title: Authenticate users and route requests to agents in a fleet with ASP.NET Core
+description: Validate user access tokens once for a shared ASP.NET Core runtime, route each request to an agent, and enforce per-agent access.
+titleSuffix: Microsoft Entra Agent ID
+ms.topic: how-to
+ms.date: 11/05/2026
+ms.reviewer: dastrock
+ai-usage: ai-assisted
+
+#customer-intent: As a developer building an agent hosting platform with ASP.NET Core, I want to authenticate users and make sure they can only reach the agents they're allowed to use.
+---
+
+# Authenticate users and route requests to agents in a fleet with ASP.NET Core
+
+Users call a fleet agent with an access token for the blueprint's `access_agent` scope. Every agent in the fleet shares that audience, so token validation proves who the user is but not which agent they're allowed to use. The runtime routes each request to an agent and enforces per-agent access itself.
+
+## Prerequisites
+
+- Complete [Call APIs as an agent in a fleet with ASP.NET Core](aspnet-core-fleet-call-apis-as-agent.md).
+- The `access_agent` scope [exposed on the blueprint](set-up-blueprint-agent-fleet.md#expose-the-inbound-scope).
+- An upstream client that signs in users and requests the scope `api://<agent-identity-blueprint-client-id>/access_agent`.
+
+## Configure token validation
+
+Token validation is the same as for a single agent. Use the blueprint client ID as the expected audience. For upstream client setup and validation details, see [Authenticate users to an ASP.NET Core agent API](aspnet-core-authenticate-users.md).
+
+To limit which users can call the fleet at all, [require an app role assignment](control-user-access-agents.md) on the blueprint principal. Those app roles apply to every agent in the fleet.
+
+## Enforce per-agent access
+
+Decide who can use each agent, and store that decision in the runtime. For example, record the users and groups that an agent's owner shares it with. Define an access policy that the runtime checks on every request:
+
+```csharp
+using System.Security.Claims;
+
+public interface IAgentAccessPolicy
+{
+    Task<bool> CanUseAgentAsync(ClaimsPrincipal user, string agentId);
+}
+```
+
+Identify the user by the `tid` and `oid` claims. Don't use the user principal name or email as a stable key.
+
+Implement `IAgentAccessPolicy` against your sharing records and register it in dependency injection before mapping the endpoint. The interface alone doesn't enforce access.
+
+## Route requests to agents
+
+Put the runtime's agent ID in the route. Validate the token, confirm the agent exists, and check the access policy before running the agent:
+
+```csharp
+using Microsoft.Identity.Web.Resource;
+
+app.MapPost("/agents/{agentId}/messages", async (
+    string agentId,
+    HttpContext context,
+    IAgentDirectory directory,
+    IAgentAccessPolicy accessPolicy) =>
+{
+    context.VerifyUserHasAnyAcceptedScope("access_agent");
+
+    if (await directory.FindAsync(agentId) is null
+        || !await accessPolicy.CanUseAgentAsync(context.User, agentId))
+    {
+        return Results.NotFound();
+    }
+
+    // Run the agent for this request.
+    return Results.Accepted();
+})
+.RequireAuthorization();
+```
+
+The endpoint returns `404 Not Found` both for an unknown agent and for an agent the user can't use, so callers can't discover other agents in the fleet. After these checks pass, use `agentId` for every token request made while handling the request.
+
+Before adding agent work, test with a user who can access one agent but not another. The allowed request reaches the placeholder `202 Accepted` response; requests for the other agent and an unknown agent return `404 Not Found`. Confirm that neither rejected request runs agent work or requests a downstream token. The placeholder response verifies routing and access checks, not agent execution.
+
+## Next step
+
+[Call APIs as a user in a fleet with ASP.NET Core](aspnet-core-fleet-call-apis-as-user.md)
+

+- [Plan an agent fleet on a shared runtime](plan-agent-fleet.md)

+---
+title: Call APIs as an agent's user account in a fleet with ASP.NET Core
+description: Select the agent identity and agent's user account for each token request in a shared ASP.NET Core runtime that hosts many agents.
+titleSuffix: Microsoft Entra Agent ID
+ms.topic: how-to
+ms.date: 11/05/2026
+ms.reviewer: dastrock
+ai-usage: ai-assisted
+
+#customer-intent: As a developer building an agent hosting platform with ASP.NET Core, I want agents in my fleet to call Microsoft 365 as their own agent's user accounts.
+---
+
+# Call APIs as an agent's user account in a fleet with ASP.NET Core
+
+Some agents in a fleet need a user object for Microsoft 365 workloads, such as a mailbox or Teams membership. For those agents, look up both the agent identity and its agent's user account in the agent directory, and pass them to `WithAgentUserIdentity`.
+
+To decide whether an agent needs an agent's user account, see [Use an agent's user account with Microsoft 365](agent-user-oauth-flow.md#determine-whether-the-agent-needs-a-user-object).
+
+## Prerequisites
+
+- Complete [Call APIs as an agent in a fleet with ASP.NET Core](aspnet-core-fleet-call-apis-as-agent.md).
+- An agent's user account [provisioned for the agent](aspnet-core-fleet-provision-agent-identities.md#provision-an-agent).
+- Delegated permissions for the target API, such as `Mail.ReadWrite`, [granted to the agent identity](grant-agent-access-microsoft-365.md) or [inherited from the blueprint](set-up-blueprint-agent-fleet.md#optionally-configure-inheritable-permissions).
+- The Microsoft 365 licenses and resource access that the agent's user account needs. For details, see [Provision access](agent-user-oauth-flow.md#provision-access).
+
+## Get a token for an agent's user account
+
+Add a method to `FleetTokenService`:
+
+```csharp
+using System.Security.Claims;
+
+public async Task<string> CreateAuthorizationHeaderForAgentUserAsync(
+    string agentId, string scope)
+{
+    AgentRegistration registration = await GetRegistrationAsync(agentId);
+
+    if (registration.AgentUserId is null)
+    {
+        throw new InvalidOperationException(
+            $"Agent '{agentId}' doesn't have an agent's user account.");
+    }
+
+    var options = new AuthorizationHeaderProviderOptions()
+        .WithAgentUserIdentity(
+            registration.AgentIdentityId,
+            Guid.Parse(registration.AgentUserId));
+
+    return await authorizationHeaderProvider
+        .CreateAuthorizationHeaderForUserAsync([scope], options, new ClaimsPrincipal());
+}
+```
+
+Pass `new ClaimsPrincipal()` because no person is signed in. The user comes from the agent directory, not from the request context.
+
+Call the method from the agent's work, and send the header to Microsoft Graph:
+
+```csharp
+using System.Net.Http.Headers;
+
+string authorizationHeader = await fleetTokenService
+    .CreateAuthorizationHeaderForAgentUserAsync(agentId, "https://graph.microsoft.com/.default");
+
+HttpClient client = httpClientFactory.CreateClient();
+client.DefaultRequestHeaders.Authorization =
+    AuthenticationHeaderValue.Parse(authorizationHeader);
+
+using HttpResponseMessage response =
+    await client.GetAsync("https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/me/messages");
+response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();
+```
+
+The token represents the agent's user account, so `/me` returns that account's data. Each agent can reach only the mailbox, files, and teams that its own account was given.
+
+For this example, verify that Microsoft Graph returns a successful messages response for the selected agent's mailbox. An empty messages collection isn't an authentication failure. If the call fails, check delegated permission grants separately from the account's license, mailbox provisioning, and resource access; acquiring a token doesn't provision a mailbox.
+
+## Next step
+
+[Authenticate users and route requests to agents in a fleet with ASP.NET Core](aspnet-core-fleet-authenticate-users.md)
+
+## Related content
+
+- [Use an agent's user account with Microsoft 365](agent-user-oauth-flow.md)
+- [Agent's user accounts](agent-users.md)
+- [Plan an agent fleet on a shared runtime](plan-agent-fleet.md)

@@ -0,0 +1,190 @@
+---
+title: Call APIs as an agent in a fleet with ASP.NET Core
+description: Select the agent identity for each app-only token request in a shared ASP.NET Core runtime that hosts many agents.
+titleSuffix: Microsoft Entra Agent ID
+ms.topic: how-to
+ms.date: 11/05/2026
+ms.reviewer: dastrock
+ai-usage: ai-assisted
+
+#customer-intent: As a developer building an agent hosting platform with ASP.NET Core, I want each agent in my fleet to call APIs with its own agent identity.
+---
+
+# Call APIs as an agent in a fleet with ASP.NET Core
+
+In a fleet, the runtime acquires app-only tokens for many agents with one blueprint credential. Look up the agent's identity in the agent directory, and pass it to `WithAgentIdentity` on each token request. The token request is otherwise the same as for a single agent.
+
+## Prerequisites
+
+- Complete [Provision agent identities for a fleet with ASP.NET Core](aspnet-core-fleet-provision-agent-identities.md).
+- Application permissions for the target API, [granted to the agent identity](grant-application-permissions-agent-identity.md) or [inherited from the blueprint](set-up-blueprint-agent-fleet.md#optionally-configure-inheritable-permissions).
+- A Redis service reachable from the runtime. Set `Redis:ConnectionString` in the runtime's configuration, using your hosting platform's protected configuration for connection credentials.
+
+## Install the packages
+
+```dotnetcli
+dotnet add package Microsoft.Identity.Web
+dotnet add package Microsoft.Identity.Web.AgentIdentities
+dotnet add package Microsoft.Extensions.Caching.StackExchangeRedis
+```
+
+## Configure the runtime
+
+Use the same `AzureAd` section and blueprint credential as the provisioning service. Register Agent ID support and a distributed token cache:
+
+Apply these registrations before `builder.Build()` in your ASP.NET Core runtime. The snippets extend that project; they aren't a complete `Program.cs`. Keep its startup pipeline and register the persistent `IAgentDirectory` implementation from the provisioning step.
+
+```csharp
+using Microsoft.Identity.Web;
+
+var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);
+
+builder.Services
+    .AddMicrosoftIdentityWebApiAuthentication(builder.Configuration)
+    .EnableTokenAcquisitionToCallDownstreamApi()
+    .AddDistributedTokenCaches();
+
+builder.Services.AddStackExchangeRedisCache(options =>
+    options.Configuration = builder.Configuration["Redis:ConnectionString"]);
+
+builder.Services.AddAgentIdentities();
+builder.Services.AddHttpClient();
+builder.Services.AddAuthorization();
+builder.Services.AddScoped<FleetTokenService>();
+// Register your IAgentDirectory implementation.
+```
+
+The runtime caches tokens for every agent identity in the fleet. Use a distributed token cache so the cache is shared across runtime instances and survives restarts. For options, see [Token cache serialization](/entra/msal/dotnet/how-to/token-cache-serialization).
+
+## Get a token for an agent
+
+Create a service that resolves the agent identity and acquires a token for it. The runtime passes its own agent ID, never an agent identity client ID taken from a request or from agent output.
+
+```csharp
+using Microsoft.Identity.Abstractions;
+using Microsoft.Identity.Web;
+
+public class FleetTokenService(
+    IAgentDirectory directory,
+    IAuthorizationHeaderProvider authorizationHeaderProvider)
+{
+    public async Task<string> CreateAuthorizationHeaderForAgentAsync(
+        string agentId, string scope)
+    {
+        AgentRegistration registration = await GetRegistrationAsync(agentId);
+
+        var options = new AuthorizationHeaderProviderOptions()
+            .WithAgentIdentity(registration.AgentIdentityId);
+
+        return await authorizationHeaderProvider
+            .CreateAuthorizationHeaderForAppAsync(scope, options);
+    }
+
+    private async Task<AgentRegistration> GetRegistrationAsync(string agentId) =>
+        await directory.FindAsync(agentId)
+            ?? throw new InvalidOperationException($"Agent '{agentId}' isn't provisioned.");
+}
+```
+
+Call the service from the code that runs the agent's work, such as a scheduled job or message handler:
+
+```csharp
+using System.Net.Http.Headers;
+
+string authorizationHeader = await fleetTokenService
+    .CreateAuthorizationHeaderForAgentAsync(agentId, "api://<custom-api-client-id>/.default");
+
+HttpClient client = httpClientFactory.CreateClient();
+client.DefaultRequestHeaders.Authorization =
+    AuthenticationHeaderValue.Parse(authorizationHeader);
+
+using HttpResponseMessage response =
+    await client.GetAsync("https://api.contoso.com/data");
+response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();
+```
+
+Don't expose `FleetTokenService` to agent code that the runtime doesn't trust. Code that can call it can request a token for any agent in the fleet.
+
+## Call specific resources
+
+Use the resource scopes and permission setup from the linked articles, while keeping the fleet's blueprint configuration and `AddAgentIdentities` registration. The single-instance samples use the configured client ID directly and omit identity overrides. For each fleet request, use `FleetTokenService` to select the directory entry. The Microsoft Graph and Azure SDK examples in this article show explicit SDK options.
+
+| Resource | Scope | Guidance |
+| --- | --- | --- |
+| Custom API | `api://<custom-api-client-id>/.default` | [Call a custom API as an agent](call-api-custom.md) |
+| Azure services | The service's `.default` scope, such as `https://storage.azure.com/.default` | [Call Azure services as an agent](call-api-azure-services.md) |
+| Microsoft Graph | `https://graph.microsoft.com/.default` | [Call Microsoft Graph as an agent](call-api-microsoft-graph.md) |
+
+### Use the Microsoft Graph SDK
+
+Install `Microsoft.Identity.Web.GraphServiceClient` and register the client:
+
+```dotnetcli
+dotnet add package Microsoft.Identity.Web.GraphServiceClient
+```
+
+```csharp
+builder.Services.AddMicrosoftGraph(options =>
+{
+    options.BaseUrl = "https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0";
+    options.Scopes = ["https://graph.microsoft.com/.default"];
+});
+```
+
+After resolving `registration` from the directory in trusted runtime code, select that agent on each Graph request:
+
+```csharp
+using Microsoft.Graph;
+using Microsoft.Identity.Web;
+
+var users = await graphClient.Users.GetAsync(request =>
+    request.Options.WithAuthenticationOptions(options =>
+    {
+        options.RequestAppToken = true;
+        options.WithAgentIdentity(registration.AgentIdentityId);
+    }));
+```
+
+The operation requires an application permission such as `User.Read.All`. Don't remove `WithAgentIdentity` when adapting the single-instance Graph sample.
+
+### Use an Azure SDK client
+
+Install the identity integration and the resource SDK, and register the credential:
+
+```dotnetcli
+dotnet add package Microsoft.Identity.Web.Azure
+dotnet add package Azure.Storage.Blobs
+```
+
+```csharp
+builder.Services.AddMicrosoftIdentityAzureTokenCredential();
+```
+
+For each agent operation, create a separate dependency injection scope. Set `MicrosoftIdentityTokenCredential.Options.RequestAppToken` to `true` for app-only access, and pass the resolved `registration.AgentIdentityId` to `credential.Options.WithAgentIdentity`. This selects the fleet agent whose token the Azure SDK client requests:
+
+```csharp
+using Azure.Storage.Blobs;
+using Microsoft.Identity.Web;
+
+using IServiceScope agentScope = serviceScopeFactory.CreateScope();
+var credential = agentScope.ServiceProvider
+    .GetRequiredService<MicrosoftIdentityTokenCredential>();
+credential.Options.RequestAppToken = true;
+credential.Options.WithAgentIdentity(registration.AgentIdentityId);
+
+var blobs = new BlobServiceClient(
+    new Uri("https://<storage-account>.blob.core.windows.net"),
+    credential);
+var properties = await blobs.GetPropertiesAsync();
+```
+
+Inject `IServiceScopeFactory` as `serviceScopeFactory`. The credential has mutable options: don't share it or its Azure SDK client across agents, and finish the operation before disposing the scope. Assign the required Azure role to the agent identity, not to the blueprint or the runtime's managed identity.
+
+## Next step
+
+[Call APIs as an agent's user account in a fleet with ASP.NET Core](aspnet-core-fleet-call-apis-as-agent-user.md)
+
+## Related content
+
+- [Plan an agent fleet on a shared runtime](plan-agent-fleet.md)
+- [Validate Agent ID tokens in a downstream API](how-to-validate-agent-tokens-downstream-api.md)
