-#customer intent: As a developer or architect building AI agents, I want to understand how Microsoft Entra ID Auth SDK (sidecar) handles authentication so that I can keep credentials out of agent code while giving each agent its own auditable identity.
-
+#customer-intent: As an agent developer, I want to understand the Auth SDK sidecar so that my agent can use Microsoft Entra authentication without handling credentials or tokens directly.
 ---
 
-# Authentication with Microsoft Entra ID Auth SDK (sidecar)
-
-The [Microsoft Entra ID Auth SDK (sidecar)](https://mcr.microsoft.com/en-us/product/entra-sdk/auth-sidecar/about) handles authentication and token operations for your AI agent. It runs as a second container next to your agent that handles client-credentials exchange, on-behalf-of flows, and token lifecycle management. This article explains the Microsoft Entra ID Auth SDK (sidecar) design pattern, how it works, and the identity objects involved. 
-
-## Why use the Microsoft Entra ID Auth SDK (sidecar)?
-
-AI agents need credentials to call downstream APIs, but the common approaches to agent authentication fall short:
-
-- **Hard-coded secrets in agent code:** Every agent image holds a copy of your app's `client_secret`. Any compromise, log leak, or forgotten `.env` file committed to Git exposes the full tenant.
-- **Delegated user tokens for everything:** The agent can only act when a human is present. You also lose individual auditability because every call looks like the same service principal.
+# Authentication with Microsoft Entra ID Auth SDK sidecar
 
-Microsoft Entra Agent ID gives each agent its own identity. The sidecar pattern makes that identity easy to use by keeping all credential handling outside your agent code.
+Use the Microsoft Entra ID Auth SDK sidecar when your cloud agent isn't built with ASP.NET Core and Microsoft.Identity.Web. The sidecar runs next to the agent, holds the blueprint credential, acquires and caches tokens, and returns authorization headers or calls downstream APIs.
 
-## How the Microsoft Entra ID Auth SDK (sidecar) works
+The agent communicates with the sidecar through `localhost` in a shared network namespace. Don't expose the sidecar endpoint publicly.
 
-The [Microsoft Entra ID Auth SDK (sidecar)](https://mcr.microsoft.com/en-us/product/entra-sdk/auth-sidecar/about) runs as a container that exposes HTTP endpoints on the pod-local network. It handles the following responsibilities:
+## Choose this integration
 
-- Exchanges client credentials with `login.microsoftonline.com`.
-- Acquires tokens through client credentials or federated identity credentials (FIC) for the agent identity in autonomous flows.
-- Handles on-behalf-of (OBO) flows for user-context calls.
-- Caches tokens and manages refresh and expiry.
-- Abstracts the credential source - uses `ClientSecret` for development and `SignedAssertionFromManagedIdentity` for Azure deployments through the same API.
+Use the sidecar when the agent needs to:
 
-The following table summarizes the flow of auth actions between your agent and the sidecar:
+- Call an API as its Agent ID.
+- Call an API as a signed-in user through On-Behalf-Of (OBO).
+- Validate an incoming user token and read its claims.
+- Change credential sources without changing agent code.
 
-| Agent (your code) | Microsoft Entra ID Auth SDK (sidecar) |
-|---|---|
-| Decide when to call the API | Acquire and cache the right token |
-| Build the HTTP request | Perform client-credentials and OBO exchange |
-| Pass through user token for OBO | Validate and forward user assertion |
-| Handle business logic | Communicate with `login.microsoftonline.com` |
+For ASP.NET Core agents, use the integrated Microsoft.Identity.Web guidance in this documentation instead.
 
-The security boundary is explicit: the sidecar has no host port. Only services inside the same network, such as your agent container, can request tokens.
+## How the sidecar works
 
-## Identity objects in the sidecar pattern
+| Component | Responsibility |
+| --- | --- |
+| Upstream client | Signs in a user and sends an access token to the agent when user context is required. |
+| Agent | Applies business logic and requests an authorization header or downstream call. |
+| Sidecar | Validates inbound tokens, authenticates with the configured shared client ID and blueprint credential, and caches tokens. |
+| Protected API | Validates the resulting access token and authorizes the request. |
 
-The following table describes the Microsoft Entra objects in the sidecar pattern:
+For a cloud agent, the sidecar supports two token acquisition patterns:
 
-| Object | Role | Location |
-|---|---|---|
-| **Blueprint application** | Template that creates and issues agent identities. Holds the client credential (secret or federated). | Your Microsoft Entra tenant |
-| **Agent identity** | The individual AI agent. Has a unique app ID, permission grants, and audit trail. | Your Microsoft Entra tenant |
-| **Client single-page application (SPA)** (OBO only) | Web UI that signs the user in and exchanges the user's token for an agent token on their behalf. | Your Microsoft Entra tenant |
-| **Sidecar container** | Runs client-credentials and OBO flows. Holds the blueprint credential. | Next to your agent |
-| **Agent container** | Your application code. Requests authorization headers from the sidecar. | Your pod, compose service, or App Service |
+- **App-only Agent ID:** The agent requests a token without an inbound user token.
+- **Agent acting for a signed-in user:** The agent forwards the inbound user token and the sidecar performs OBO.
 
-For more information about blueprints and agent identities, see [Agent identity blueprints](agent-blueprint.md) and [Agent identities](what-are-agent-identities.md).
+If you're building a platform that hosts separate agents for teams or customers, or your scenario needs an agent's dedicated user account, follow the [agent fleet tutorial](sidecar-fleet-provision-agent-identities.md).
 
-## Credential source abstraction
+The following diagram shows an agent and sidecar running in the same private environment. The agent requests an authorization header from the sidecar, which gets an access token from Microsoft Entra.
 
-The sidecar abstracts the credential source from your agent code. During development, you can use a `ClientSecret` for convenience. In production Azure deployments, you can switch to `SignedAssertionFromManagedIdentity`, a federated identity credential backed by managed identity, without changing your agent code.
+:::image type="content" source="media/configure-third-party-agents/sidecar-pattern-architecture.png" alt-text="Diagram that shows an agent requesting an authorization header from a sidecar, which obtains an access token from Microsoft Entra ID." lightbox="media/configure-third-party-agents/sidecar-pattern-architecture.png" border="false":::
 
-The sidecar's configuration determines which credential source to use. Your agent continues to call the same `/AuthorizationHeader` endpoint regardless of the authentication mechanism.
+## Security boundary
 
-## Sidecar sample scenarios
+Run the sidecar in the same network namespace as the agent, such as the same pod or container app. Production builds restrict callers to loopback; separate containers on a private bridge aren't sufficient. For Docker Compose, follow the [shared-network configuration](microsoft-entra-sdk-for-agent-identities.md#add-the-sidecar-container). Only trusted agent code should be able to call it. Use a managed identity and federated identity credential for hosted deployments. Use client secrets only for local development.
 
-The [Microsoft Entra Agent ID sidecar samples](https://github.com/microsoft/entra-agentid-samples/tree/dev/sidecar) demonstrate the following concepts:
+## Next steps
 
-- How a blueprint differs from an agent identity and why agents need their own identity.
-- How the sidecar exposes `/AuthorizationHeader` (get token) and `/DownstreamApi` (token + proxied call) endpoints.
-- How the sidecar forwards a signed-in user's token and has the Microsoft Entra ID Auth SDK (sidecar) mint an agent-on-behalf-of-user token via OBO.
-- How the downstream API validates agent tokens including the signature, issuer, `xms_par_app_azp`, and audience.
-- How to swap from `ClientSecret` (development) to `SignedAssertionFromManagedIdentity` (Azure deployments) without changing agent code.
+1. [Configure the Auth SDK sidecar](microsoft-entra-sdk-for-agent-identities.md).
+1. [Run the sidecar locally](sidecar-local-development.md).
+1. [Call a custom API as the agent](sidecar-call-custom-api-as-agent.md).

 #customer intent: As a developer or IT administrator, I want to understand authorization controls for agent IDs so that I can properly configure roles and permissions while maintaining security boundaries for AI agents in my organization.
 ---
 
 # Authorization in Microsoft Entra Agent ID
 
-The introduction of agent identities is driven by the rise of AI-powered agents in organizations. Traditional identity types (like standard app registrations or user accounts) aren't ideal for autonomous agents. AI agents have unique security concerns because their autonomous decision-making, dynamic learning capabilities, and potentially access to sensitive data can introduce unpredictable behaviors.
+Authorize an agent according to the resource it needs to access: Azure roles govern Azure resources, Microsoft Entra roles govern directory administration, and API permissions govern calls to Microsoft Graph and other APIs. Microsoft Entra Agent ID restricts high-privilege assignments to limit what an autonomous agent can do.
 
-Microsoft Entra Agent ID was created to fill this gap. Built on the Microsoft Entra ID platform, it provides a dedicated authentication and authorization framework for AI agents that enables them to safely access services and APIs while giving administrators a central way to monitor and control their actions. -## Decide which approach to use based on your scenario
+## Prerequisites
 
-The following table helps you decide which approach to use. For most scenarios, we recommend using `IDownstreamApi`. 
+- An existing ASP.NET Core web API project and the .NET SDK for its target framework. The examples were tested with .NET 10 and Microsoft.Identity.Web 4.17.0; these are tested versions, not minimum supported versions.

+    Use the agent identity's `id` recorded during creation for `<agent-identity-object-id>`, not its shared OAuth client ID or the blueprint's object ID. Follow any `@odata.nextLink` values. Confirm that `principalId` is the agent identity's object ID, `resourceId` is the custom API's service principal object ID, and `appRoleId` is the intended role. For the required read permissions and delegated-user roles, see [List appRoleAssignments](/graph/api/serviceprincipal-list-approleassignments).

+
+## Configure ASP.NET Core
+
+In `Program.cs`, register Microsoft.Identity.Web, an HTTP client, and the inbound `AgentUser` authorization policy. This path uses ordinary confidential-client token acquisition, without `AddAgentIdentities` or `WithAgentIdentity`. The incoming caller's token is for the agent API; the downstream app-only token is for the custom API.
+
+```csharp
+using System.Net.Http.Headers;
+using Microsoft.Identity.Abstractions;
+using Microsoft.Identity.Web;
+
+var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);
+
+builder.Services
+    .AddMicrosoftIdentityWebApiAuthentication(builder.Configuration)
+    .EnableTokenAcquisitionToCallDownstreamApi()
+    .AddInMemoryTokenCaches();
+
+builder.Services.AddHttpClient();
+builder.Services.AddAuthorization(options =>
+{
+    options.AddPolicy(
+        "AgentUser",
+        policy => policy.RequireRole("Agent.User"));
+});
+
+var app = builder.Build();
+
+app.UseAuthentication();
+app.UseAuthorization();
+
+// Map the custom API endpoint before app.Run().
+app.Run();
+```
+
+## Call the API
 
-1. Configure your services to add authentication with agent identities:
-
-    ```csharp
-    using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authorization;
-    using Microsoft.Identity.Abstractions;
-    using Microsoft.Identity.Web;
-    
-    var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);
-    
-    // With Microsoft.Identity.Web
-    builder.Services.AddMicrosoftIdentityWebApiAuthentication(builder.Configuration)
-        .EnableTokenAcquisitionToCallDownstreamApi();
-    
-    builder.Services.AddAgentIdentities();
-    
-    var app = builder.Build();
-    
-    app.UseAuthentication();
-    app.UseAuthorization();
-    
-    app.Run();
+Use `IAuthorizationHeaderProvider.CreateAuthorizationHeaderForAppAsync`. Pass the custom API's `.default` scope as a string. Replace `<custom-api-application-id-uri>` with the same URI you used for consent, and replace `https://api.contoso.com/data` with the API endpoint. The provider uses the configured client ID and credential directly.
+
+Insert the following endpoint at the comment in `Program.cs`, before `app.Run()`. The required `using` directives are already at the top of the file. The endpoint gets an app-only authorization header and sends it to the custom API:
+
+```csharp
+app.MapGet("/custom-api", async (
+    IAuthorizationHeaderProvider authorizationHeaderProvider,
+    IHttpClientFactory httpClientFactory) =>
+{
+    string authorizationHeader = await authorizationHeaderProvider
+        .CreateAuthorizationHeaderForAppAsync(
+            "<custom-api-application-id-uri>/.default");
+
+    HttpClient client = httpClientFactory.CreateClient();
+    client.DefaultRequestHeaders.Authorization =
+        AuthenticationHeaderValue.Parse(authorizationHeader);
+
+    using HttpResponseMessage response =
+        await client.GetAsync("https://api.contoso.com/data");
+    response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();
+
+    return Results.Content(
+        await response.Content.ReadAsStringAsync(),
+        response.Content.Headers.ContentType?.ToString());
+})
+.RequireAuthorization("AgentUser");
+```

+The returned authorization header includes the `Bearer` scheme. Don't return tokens or authorization headers from a production endpoint.
+
+The sample requires an authenticated caller with the `Agent.User` role. Configure that assignment through the [agent's inbound access policy](control-user-access-agents.md) before allowing the caller to trigger an app-only operation.
+
+Request only the application permissions required by the endpoint. For guidance on defining and granting app roles, see [application roles](/entra/identity-platform/howto-add-app-roles-in-apps).

A downstream non-success status causes `EnsureSuccessStatusCode` to fail; this sample doesn't translate downstream errors into matching inbound status codes.
 
----
+1. Repeat the request without an authorization header: expect `401 Unauthorized` from the agent. With an otherwise valid agent API token that lacks `Agent.User`, expect `403 Forbidden` if the tenant issues that token. When assignment is required, the tenant might reject token issuance first.
+1. At the downstream API, confirm signature, issuer, audience, lifetime, and the required app role are validated. Compare the validated token's `oid` with the agent identity object ID, not the blueprint object ID, and check its `roles` claim. See [Validate Agent ID tokens in a downstream API](how-to-validate-agent-tokens-downstream-api.md). A successful token response alone doesn't prove these checks.
+1. Test the downstream API's rejection of a token without its required role, using a separate test identity or fixture rather than removing production grants. Expect rejection at that API; don't infer its status from the agent's exception response.

-# Call a Microsoft Graph API from an agent using .NET
-
-This article explains how to call a Microsoft Graph API from an agent using agent identities or an agent's user account.
-
-[!INCLUDE [Common call API content](./includes/call-api-common-dotnet.md)]
-
-## Call a Microsoft Graph API
-
-1. Install the *Microsoft.Identity.Web.GraphServiceClient* that handles authentication for the Graph SDK and the *Microsoft.Identity.Web.AgentIdentities* package to add support for agent identities.
-
-    ```bash
-    dotnet add package Microsoft.Identity.Web.GraphServiceClient
-    dotnet add package Microsoft.Identity.Web.AgentIdentities
-    ```
-
-1. Add the support for Microsoft Graph and agent identities in your service collection.
-
-    ```csharp
-    using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.OpenIdConnect;
-    using Microsoft.Identity.Web;
-    
-    var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);
-    
-    // Add authentication (web app or web API)
-    builder.Services.AddAuthentication(OpenIdConnectDefaults.AuthenticationScheme)
-        .AddMicrosoftIdentityWebApp(builder.Configuration.GetSection("AzureAd"))
-        .EnableTokenAcquisitionToCallDownstreamApi()
-        .AddInMemoryTokenCaches();
-    
-    // Add Microsoft Graph support
-    builder.Services.AddMicrosoftGraph();
-    
-    // Add Agent Identities support
-    builder.Services.AddAgentIdentities();
-    
-    var app = builder.Build();
-    app.UseAuthentication();
-    app.UseAuthorization();
-    app.Run();
-    ``` 
-
-1. Configure Graph and agent identity options in *appsettings.json*.
-
-    [!INCLUDE [Dont use secrets](./includes/do-not-use-secrets.md)]
-
-    ```json
-    {
-      "AzureAd": {
-        "Instance": "https://login.microsoftonline.com/",
-        "TenantId": "<your-tenant-id>",
-        "ClientId": "<agent-blueprint-client-id>",
-        "ClientCredentials": [
-          {
-            "SourceType": "ClientSecret",
-            "ClientSecret": "your-client-secret"
-          }
-        ]
-      },
-      "DownstreamApis": {
-        "MicrosoftGraph": {
-          "BaseUrl": "https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0",
-          "Scopes": ["User.Read", "User.ReadBasic.All"]
-        }
-      }
-    }
-    ```
-
-    > [!NOTE]
-    > Configure only the Microsoft Graph permissions your agent needs, and make sure the `Scopes` you set match the Graph resources your code calls. These examples use `User.Read` and `User.ReadBasic.All`; calling other resources requires their corresponding permissions.
-
-1. You can now get the `GraphServiceClient` injecting it in your service or from the service provider and call Microsoft Graph.
-
-  - For agent identities, you can acquire either an app only token (autonomous agents) or an on-behalf of user token (interactive agents) by using the `WithAgentIdentity` method. For app only tokens, set the `RequestAppToken` property to `true`. For delegated on-behalf of user tokens, don't set the `RequestAppToken` property or explicitly set it to `false`.
-
-      ```csharp
-      using Microsoft.Graph;
-      using Microsoft.Identity.Web;
-
-      // Get the GraphServiceClient
-      GraphServiceClient graphServiceClient = serviceProvider.GetRequiredService<GraphServiceClient>();
-        
-      string agentIdentity = "agent-identity-guid";
-        
-      // Call Microsoft Graph APIs with the agent identity for app only scenario
-      var usersAppOnly = await graphServiceClient.Users
-          .GetAsync(r => r.Options.WithAuthenticationOptions(options =>
-          {
-              options.WithAgentIdentity(agentIdentity);
-              options.RequestAppToken = true; // Set to true for app only
-          }));
-
-      // Call Microsoft Graph APIs with the agent identity for on-behalf of user scenario
-      var usersOnBehalfOfUser = await graphServiceClient.Users
-          .GetAsync(r => r.Options.WithAuthenticationOptions(options =>
-          {
-              options.WithAgentIdentity(agentIdentity);
-              options.RequestAppToken = false; // False to show it's on-behalf of user
-          }));
-      ```
-
-    - For agent's user account identities, you can specify either User Principal Name (UPN) or Object Identity (OID) to identify the agent's user account by using the `WithAgentUserIdentity` method.

+# Call Microsoft Graph as an agent with ASP.NET Core
+
+List directory users with the agent's application permissions, not the inbound caller's delegated access.
+
+In this article, you configure `GraphServiceClient` to obtain a Microsoft Graph token for the agent while the agent API separately authorizes the caller.
+
+## Prerequisites
+
+- The Microsoft Graph application permissions required by the operation.
+- Application permissions granted to the agent identity with admin consent. See [Grant Microsoft Graph application permissions to an agent identity](grant-application-permissions-agent-identity.md).
+- The [blueprint credential and ASP.NET Core services](call-api-custom.md#configure-the-blueprint-credential), including token acquisition and the `AgentUser` inbound authorization policy. Reuse its local certificate configuration for workstation testing. You don't need that walkthrough's custom API app role or consent grant for this Microsoft Graph example.
+
+## Add Microsoft Graph
+
+Install the integration package:
+
+```dotnetcli
+dotnet add package Microsoft.Identity.Web.GraphServiceClient
+```
+
+Register `GraphServiceClient` with the services configured in the parent article. For app-only access, call `builder.Services.AddMicrosoftGraph` with `options.BaseUrl` set to `https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0` and `options.Scopes` set to `["https://graph.microsoft.com/.default"]`. Use the configured client ID directly; don't add `WithAgentIdentity`.
+
+Place this registration before `builder.Build()` in the agent API's `Program.cs`.
+
+```csharp
+builder.Services.AddMicrosoftGraph(options =>
+{
+    options.BaseUrl = "https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0";
+    options.Scopes = ["https://graph.microsoft.com/.default"];
+});
+```
+
+## Call Microsoft Graph
+
+Set `RequestAppToken` to `true` so `GraphServiceClient` acquires an app-only token for the agent identity:
+
+Merge the following `using` directives with those at the top of `Program.cs`, and insert the endpoint before its single `app.Run()`. You can omit the custom API endpoint.
+
+```csharp
+using Microsoft.Graph;
+using Microsoft.Identity.Web;
+
+app.MapGet("/graph-users", async (GraphServiceClient graphClient) =>
+{
+    var users = await graphClient.Users.GetAsync(request =>
+        request.Options.WithAuthenticationOptions(options =>
+        {
+            options.RequestAppToken = true;
+        }));
+
+    return Results.Ok(users?.Value);
+})
+.RequireAuthorization("AgentUser");
+```
+
+The client uses the shared client ID and blueprint credential configured in the parent article. Don't add an Agent ID override. The example requires an application permission that can list users, such as `User.Read.All`. Grant only the permissions required by your calls.
+
+## Verify the Graph call
+
+Follow the parent journey's [API access test](call-api-custom.md#verify-api-access), replacing `/custom-api` with `/graph-users`. Expect `200` and a JSON collection of users when the agent has the required Graph application permission. This endpoint returns the first response page, not necessarily every user in the directory.
+
+Without an inbound token, expect `401`. With an otherwise valid token missing `Agent.User`, expect `403` if the tenant issues that token. A downstream Graph failure causes the sample to throw rather than returning that same status from the agent. Verify Graph consent on the agent identity separately from the caller's role assignment.
+

+
+[Authenticate users to the agent API](aspnet-core-authenticate-users.md)

-#Customer intent: As an IT admin or developer, I want to understand what happens when I delete an agent identity blueprint so I can plan for cleanup and restoration.
+#Customer intent: As an IT admin or developer, I want to understand the documented deletion and recovery behavior for agent identity objects so I can plan cleanup without assuming undocumented cascade behavior.
 ---
 
 # Agent identity deletion
 
-When you delete an agent identity blueprint or its principal, Microsoft Entra automatically cleans up all child agent identities and agents' user accounts with a *cascade cleanup* process. You don't need to manually query and delete each one. Understanding when and how this cascade cleanup happens helps you plan for restoration if needed.
+Microsoft Graph documents soft deletion and recovery for agent identity and application objects. Its public delete API references don't specify whether deleting an agent identity blueprint or blueprint principal also deletes child agent identities or associated agent user accounts. Don't rely on a cascade unless Microsoft confirms the behavior for your scenario.
 
-Agent identity blueprints and their associated objects follow the same soft deletion and hard deletion behavior as other app registrations and service principals in Microsoft Entra. For a full overview of that process, see [Deleting and recovering applications FAQ](../identity/enterprise-apps/delete-recover-faq.yml). This article focuses on what's unique to agent identity deletion.
+For general application soft-deletion behavior, see [Deleting and recovering applications FAQ](../identity/enterprise-apps/delete-recover-faq.yml). This article separates the behavior documented for individual Graph objects from related-object behavior that isn't specified in those API references.
 
 ## Object relationships
 
-The following objects are involved in the agent identity deletion lifecycle. The cascade cleanup process is based on these relationships.
-
-| Object | Directory object type | Relationship |
+| Object | Directory object type | Documented relationship or operation |
 |---|---|---|
-| Agent identity blueprint | Application | Parent of the blueprint principal |
-| Agent identity blueprint principal | Service principal | The principal for the blueprint |
-| Agent identity | Service principal | Child of the blueprint principal |
-| Agent's user account | User | Paired 1:1 with an agent identity |
+| Agent identity blueprint | Application | Delete the application object by using the Graph application delete API. |
+| Agent identity blueprint principal | Service principal | Delete the service principal by using the Graph servicePrincipal delete API. |
+| Agent identity | `agentIdentity` service principal | The `agentIdentityBlueprintId` property identifies its blueprint. Delete an agent identity by using the Graph agentIdentity delete API. |
+| Agent user | `agentUser`, a specialized user subtype | The [agentUser resource](/graph/api/resources/agentuser?view=graph-rest-beta&preserve-view=true) has a one-to-one relationship with a parent agent identity. The agentIdentity delete API doesn't specify what happens to the associated agent user. Check that object separately. |
 
 ## Disable versus delete
 
 Before deleting a blueprint, consider whether disabling is the right action instead.
 
-- **Disable**: Prevents the blueprint principal or its agent identities from authenticating, but leaves all objects in place. Use this when you want to temporarily stop agent activity, investigate an issue, or decommission agents gradually. Objects remain in the directory and count toward quota.
-- **Delete**: Removes the agent identity blueprint or its agent identity blueprint principal from the directory and triggers cascade cleanup of child agent identities. Use this when you're permanently retiring a blueprint and all agents created from it. Deletion can't be undone after the 30-day soft-deletion window expires.
-
-For information on disabling agent identities, see [Disable agent identities](disable-agent-identities.md).
-
-## Cascade cleanup
-
-When you delete an agent identity blueprint or its agent identity blueprint principal, Microsoft Entra automatically soft deletes all associated child agent identities and agents' user accounts. This cleanup is asynchronous.
-
-The cascade process works as follows:
+- **Disable**: Prevents the blueprint principal or its agent identities from authenticating, but leaves objects in place. Use this when you want to temporarily stop agent activity or investigate an issue. For more information, see [Disable agent identities](disable-agent-identities.md).
+- **Delete**: Sends a delete request for the specific Graph object addressed. The [application delete API](/graph/api/application-delete) documents a 30-day recovery period for deleted applications. The [agentIdentity delete API](/graph/api/agentidentity-delete?view=graph-rest-beta&preserve-view=true) documents the same period for deleted agent identities.
 
-1. **You delete the agent identity blueprint or agent identity blueprint principal**: The object is soft deleted and moves to the recycle bin.
-1. **Microsoft Entra triggers automatic cleanup**: A background task soft deletes all child agent identities and agents' user accounts associated with the deleted blueprint.
-1. **Objects are restorable for 30 days**: Soft-deleted objects can be restored within 30 days. After that, they're permanently deleted.
+## Related-object cleanup and restoration
 
-> [!IMPORTANT]
-> If you restore the agent identity blueprint principal before the background cleanup runs, child agent identities aren't affected. After the cleanup runs, each child identity must be restored individually. Restoring the agent identity blueprint principal doesn't reverse cascade deletions that already occurred.
+Use the API that matches the object you intend to delete:
 
-### Cascade cleanup in audit logs
+- Delete a blueprint application with `DELETE /applications/{applicationObjectId}`.
+- Delete a blueprint principal with `DELETE /servicePrincipals/{servicePrincipalId}`.
+- Delete one agent identity with `DELETE /servicePrincipals/{id}/microsoft.graph.agentIdentity`.
 
-When the background cleanup task deletes agent identities, the deletions appear in your tenant's [Microsoft Entra audit logs](~/identity/monitoring-health/concept-audit-logs.md). These entries have the following characteristics:
+The public Graph API references describe deletion of the addressed object. They don't specify whether deleting a blueprint application or principal triggers cleanup of child agent identities or associated agent users. The [Graph restore API](/graph/api/directory-deleteditems-restore) specifies that restoring an application doesn't automatically restore its associated service principal; restore that principal separately. The API references don't specify cleanup timing, an internal cleanup actor, or whether restoring a parent restores or reverses changes to child objects.
 
-| Audit log field | Value |
-|---|---|
-| **Activity** | Delete service principal |
-| **Initiated by (actor)** | Application: *Delete Agent Identities Task* |
-| **Actor App ID** | (blank) |
+Before deletion, record the object IDs you might need to recover. After the operation, check each related object independently. If an object was soft deleted, restore that object by its own ID; don't assume that restoring a blueprint or its principal restores related objects.
 
-The actor is shown as an application named **Delete Agent Identities Task** with no app ID. This is expected because the cleanup is performed by an internal Microsoft Entra background process, not by an external application or user.
+For restore steps, see [Delete and restore agent identity objects](howto-delete-agent-identity.md).
 
-> [!NOTE]
-> The cascade cleanup runs asynchronously after the blueprint is deleted. It might not run immediately — there can be a delay of hours or days between the blueprint deletion and the cleanup of child agent identities. Each child identity deletion appears as a separate audit log entry.
+## Audit logs
 
-## Orphaned objects and quota considerations
+Review the tenant's [Microsoft Entra audit logs](~/identity/monitoring-health/concept-audit-logs.md) to investigate recorded directory operations. The Graph delete API references don't specify a particular internal cleanup actor or audit sequence for related objects.
 
-When an agent identity blueprint principal is permanently deleted, any associated agent identities and agents' user accounts that weren't deleted become **orphaned objects** and become soft-deleted. Orphaned objects can't authenticate but continue to count toward directory quota until they're permanently deleted after the 30-day retention period expires.
+## Quota considerations
 
-Agent identity deletion follows the same quota rules as other Microsoft Entra objects. Soft-deleted objects continue to count toward quota limits until permanently deleted. For general quota information, see [Microsoft Entra service limits and restrictions](~/identity/users/directory-service-limits-restrictions.md).
+The public Graph API references document soft deletion and a 30-day recovery period for agent identities and applications. They don't specify an agent identity-specific quota, a maximum number of agent identities per blueprint, a maximum number of inheritable resource apps, or when quota becomes available after deletion. Check current Microsoft Entra service limits and confirm Agent ID-specific limits before capacity planning. Don't assume that soft deletion immediately frees quota.
 
-One consideration specific to agent identities: if you're using app-only permissions and are at the 250 agent identity limit for a blueprint, deleting an agent identity doesn't free up space until it's permanently deleted. By default, permanent deletion happens automatically after the 30-day retention period expires. If you need to free up quota immediately, you can force permanent deletion of soft-deleted agent identities. For steps, see [Permanently delete agent identity objects](howto-delete-agent-identity.md#permanently-delete-agent-identity-objects). Agent identity blueprints also follow this 250 limit when using app-only permissions.
+For general directory limits, see [Microsoft Entra service limits and restrictions](~/identity/users/directory-service-limits-restrictions.md).

+- [Delete and restore agent identity objects](howto-delete-agent-identity.md)
 - [Deleting and recovering applications FAQ](../identity/enterprise-apps/delete-recover-faq.yml)
 - [Microsoft Entra service limits and restrictions](../identity/users/directory-service-limits-restrictions.md)

+Permission inheritance applies to fleets that use a multi-instance blueprint and blueprint principal. A cloud or local single-instance agent has no blueprint principal and receives [permission grants directly](authenticate-single-instance-agent.md). It can still declare required resource access, but those declarations alone don't grant access.

It's expressed as a set of target resource applications and the specific delegated scopes and application roles the agent requests.

+Configure inheritable permissions on an agent identity blueprint to specify which delegated scopes can be inherited by agent identities. A scope is eligible for inheritance only when the resource app is configured as inheritable and the scope is granted to the blueprint principal.

 ## Prerequisites
 
-- An existing agent identity blueprint already created and configured
-- Either of the following permissions:
-    - Agent ID Developer role for managing agent identity blueprints owned by the user
-    - Agent ID Administrator role for managing agent identity blueprints
+- An existing agent identity blueprint.
+- For Microsoft Graph requests, the `AgentIdentityBlueprint.Create` permission to add an entry and `AgentIdentityBlueprint.ReadWrite.All` to update or delete an entry.
+- For delegated requests by a nonowner, the Agent ID Administrator role. Blueprint owners can manage their own blueprints.
 
 ## How inheritable permissions work
 
-During token issuance for an agent identity, the platform merges eligible inherited scopes with the agent's requested delegated scopes. Inherited scopes appear in the access token's **scp** claim and inherited roles appear in the **roles** claim. For details on inheritance conditions and the relationship between declarations, grants, and effective permissions, see [Inheritable permissions and required resource access](concept-inheritable-permissions.md).
+The public Microsoft Graph beta `inheritablePermission` resource documents delegated scope inheritance through `inheritableScopes`. The broader Agent ID permission model also describes application-role inheritance, but the public Graph reference doesn't define an application-role property or payload. Confirm the supported Graph API contract before relying on application-role inheritance.
 
-## Inheritance patterns
+For inheritance conditions and the distinction between declarations and grants, see [Inheritable permissions and required resource access](concept-inheritable-permissions.md) and the [Microsoft Graph `inheritablePermission` resource](/graph/api/resources/inheritablepermission?view=graph-rest-beta&preserve-view=true).
 
-The concept article describes inheritance patterns at a high level. The following table shows the specific `kind` values used in the API when you configure inheritance per resource app:
+## Inheritance patterns
 
-| Inheritance | Kind | Description |
-|-------------|------|-------------|
-| All Allowed | `allAllowed` | Inherit all available delegated scopes or application roles for the specified resource app. Newly granted scopes or roles on the agent identity blueprint principal are automatically included. |
-| None | `none` | Inherit no scopes or roles for the specified resource app. Use this to explicitly disable inheritance for scopes (`noScopes`) or roles (`noRoles`) independently. |
+The Graph beta API supports these patterns for delegated permission scopes:
 
-You can configure scopes and roles independently on the same resource. For example, you can inherit all scopes while inheriting no roles, or vice versa.
+| Pattern | Graph type | Description |
+| --- | --- | --- |
+| All allowed scopes | `allAllowedScopes` | Make all delegated scopes published by the resource app eligible for inheritance. |
+| Enumerated scopes | `enumeratedScopes` | Make only the listed delegated scopes eligible for inheritance. |
+| No scopes | `noScopes` | Disable delegated scope inheritance for the resource app. |
 
 ## Inheritable permissions limitations
 
-- Maximum of 50 resource apps per agent identity blueprint (for example, up to 50 entries in the *inheritablePermissions* collection). If you exceed this limit, reduce the number of resource apps to stay within the supported boundary.
+The public Microsoft Graph reference doesn't specify a maximum number of resource apps or `inheritablePermissions` entries for a blueprint. Don't rely on a numeric limit unless Microsoft publishes or confirms it.
 
-Regularly review and monitor your inheritable permissions configuration. Reevaluate inherited scopes and roles to ensure they remain appropriate for your use case. Audit which inherited scopes and roles are being used by agents and remove any unused permissions from both the agent identity blueprint principal and the inheritable permissions list to maintain security hygiene.
+The public Graph reference also doesn't document how application roles are configured for inheritance. The API examples in this article are limited to delegated scopes.
 
-## Configure inheritable permissions (using Microsoft Graph)
+Regularly review the scopes configured on each blueprint and the grants on its blueprint principal. Remove permissions that are no longer needed.
 
-To configure inheritable permissions, use the inheritablePermissions navigation property on the `agentIdentityBlueprint` application resource. Each entry specifies the scopes and roles inheritance configuration for a single resource app. Document your configuration decisions by tracking why each scope or role is inheritable and who approved it for audit purposes.
+## Configure scope inheritance (using Microsoft Graph)
 
-When specifying the `resourceAppId` in your requests, ensure you provide a valid GUID format. Invalid GUIDs result in 400 Bad Request errors.
+These examples use the Microsoft Graph beta API. Beta APIs are subject to change and aren't supported for production applications. For details, see the Microsoft Graph [create](/graph/api/agentidentityblueprint-post-inheritablepermissions?view=graph-rest-beta&preserve-view=true), [update](/graph/api/inheritablepermission-update?view=graph-rest-beta&preserve-view=true), and [delete](/graph/api/agentidentityblueprint-delete-inheritablepermissions?view=graph-rest-beta&preserve-view=true) operations.
 
-### Add all scopes and roles inheritance for Microsoft Graph
+Use the `inheritablePermissions` navigation property on the `agentIdentityBlueprint` application resource. Each entry specifies scope inheritance for one resource app. When specifying `resourceAppId`, use the resource app's application ID in GUID format.
 
-**Request**

+POST https://graph.microsoft.com/beta/applications/bc057821-f236-49d6-9f2c-1ebf43e9437a/microsoft.graph.agentIdentityBlueprint/inheritablePermissions
 Content-Type: application/json
-OData-Version: 4.0
 
 {
   "resourceAppId": "00000003-0000-0000-c000-000000000000",
   "inheritableScopes": {
-    "@odata.type": "#microsoft.graph.allAllowedScopes",

-  },

-{

-  }
-}

-#Customer intent: As an IT administrator managing agent identities, I want to control user and agent access to applications using app roles and assignment requirements, so that I can enforce least privilege access and prevent unauthorized usage of agents.
+#Customer intent: As an administrator, I want to use app roles to control which users, groups, and applications can access an agent.
 ---
 
-# Control user access to agents
+# Control access to agents with app roles
 
-This article describes how to control user and agent access to applications using app roles and the `assignmentRequired` property. It covers defining app roles, enforcing explicit role assignments, assigning roles using Microsoft Graph or the Microsoft Entra admin center, and best practices for secure access management.
+App roles define who can access an agent and what they can do. Use them to restrict agent operations to approved users, groups, or client applications.
+
+In this article, you define an inbound access role, assign it to a caller, and enforce it in the agent API. Where you define the role depends on whether the agent uses a single-instance blueprint or a fleet.
 
 ## Prerequisites
 
-- An existing agent identity blueprint already created and configured
-- Agent ID Administrator role for managing agent identities and assignments
-- Application Administrator or Cloud Application Administrator role for managing app roles and assignmentRequired properties
-- *AppRoleAssignment.ReadWrite.All* permission for Microsoft Graph API operations if using programmatic approach.
+- A blueprint and its agent API service principal.
+- An authorized Microsoft Graph management client for role configuration. For delegated single-instance management, the signed-in user must own the agent identity or have the **Agent ID Administrator** role. See [Update servicePrincipal](/graph/api/serviceprincipal-update?view=graph-rest-beta&preserve-view=true) for the applicable API permissions.
+- **Application Administrator** or **Cloud Application Administrator** to manage user and group app role assignments.
+- `AppRoleAssignment.ReadWrite.All` and the appropriate read permission for programmatic assignments.
 
-## What are app roles?
+For the single-instance cloud journey, the API's service principal is the **agent identity**, not a blueprint principal. Use its object ID as `<agent-api-service-principal-object-id>` in the requests in this article. A single-instance blueprint has no blueprint principal. For the advanced fleet journey, use the fleet's **blueprint principal** instead; its assignments apply across the fleet.
 
-App roles define logical permissions or access levels for an application. They're declared in the agent identity blueprint and can be assigned to users, groups, service principals, or agent identities. The following section shows an example app role definition:
+## Define app roles
 
-```json
-{
-  "id": "b1a2c3d4-e5f6-7890-abcd-ef1234567890",
-  "allowedMemberTypes": ["User", "Application"],
-  "description": "Grants ability to invoke agent actions",
-  "displayName": "AgentInvoker",
-  "isEnabled": true,
-  "value": "AgentInvoker"
-}
-```
+Choose the definition location for your instance mode:
 
-- `allowedMemberTypes` controls who can be assigned (users, apps, or both).
-- `value` is the string that appears in the token's roles claim when assigned.
+| Instance mode | Define the inbound role on | Assign the role on |
+| --- | --- | --- |
+| Single-instance | The blueprint application and the Agent ID service principal, using the same role GUID and value. | The Agent ID service principal. |
+| Fleet | The blueprint application. | The blueprint principal that represents the fleet API. |
 
-If an agent identity blueprint exposes no app-roles, the default app-role `<guid of all zeros>` can be used to assign principals to the agent identity.
+Use one role when everyone has the same access level. For example, use `Agent.User` for standard tasks and add `Agent.Admin` only if you expose administrative tasks. Keep role values stable because your authorization policies check them.
 
-When designing app roles for your agent applications, define granular roles that separate duties and responsibilities. For example, create specific roles like "AgentInvoker" for users who can call agent actions and "AgentAdmin" for users who can manage agent configurations. This approach provides better security control and makes it easier to audit access patterns.
+### Declare the role on the blueprint
 
-## What is assignmentRequired?
+Define `Agent.User` in the blueprint application's `appRoles` collection. For a single-instance agent, also complete the next section to make the same role available on its Agent ID.
 
-The assignmentRequired property on an application or agent identity determines whether role assignment is mandatory for access.
+Read the blueprint's existing `appRoles` first. The following request is for a blueprint with no existing roles. For an existing collection, include the existing role definitions you intend to retain; updating `appRoles` replaces the collection. Omit the read-only `origin` field from requests.
 
-- `assignmentRequired = true` → Only principals explicitly assigned an app role can sign in or call the agent identity.
-- `assignmentRequired = false` → Any authenticated principal can access the agent identity (subject to other conditions).
+Replace `<agent-user-role-id>` with a new GUID and save it for the assignment step:
 
-## Why use assignmentRequired?
-
-You might use the assignmentRequired property for the following reasons:
+```http
+PATCH https://graph.microsoft.com/beta/applications/<blueprint-object-id>
+Content-Type: application/json
+Authorization: Bearer <management-access-token>
 
-- Enforces least privilege by requiring explicit assignment.
-- Prevents accidental access by users or agents who weren't intended to use the agent.
+{
+  "@odata.type": "#microsoft.graph.agentIdentityBlueprint",
+  "appRoles": [
+    {
+      "id": "<agent-user-role-id>",
+      "allowedMemberTypes": ["User"],
+      "description": "Use standard agent features",
+      "displayName": "Agent user",
+      "isEnabled": true,
+      "value": "Agent.User"
+    }
+  ]
+}
+```
 
-Enable `assignmentRequired` for sensitive agent identity blueprints to enforce explicit role assignment and ensure only authorized principals can access critical agent functionality. If users can access an application without explicit assignment, it indicates that `assignmentRequired` is set to `false`. Change this setting to true and assign roles explicitly to maintain security controls.
+### Single-instance user access
 
-## Configure assignmentRequired
+For a single-instance agent, publish the same user role directly in the Agent ID's `appRoles` collection. Use the **same GUID and value** as the blueprint declaration, not a second role GUID. The blueprint-only declaration doesn't make the role available for assignment on the Agent ID. The service-principal-only definition doesn't complete the blueprint configuration used in this procedure.
 
-The following example uses the Update application API to set the `assignmentRequired` property.
+Read the Agent ID's existing roles first and retain their definitions in the update. For an Agent ID with no existing roles, send:
 
 ```http
-PATCH https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/applications/<agent-app-id>
+PATCH https://graph.microsoft.com/beta/servicePrincipals/<agent-api-service-principal-object-id>
 Content-Type: application/json
-Authorization: Bearer <token>
+Authorization: Bearer <management-access-token>
 
 {
-  "appRoleAssignmentRequired": true
+  "appRoles": [
+    {
+      "id": "<agent-user-role-id>",
+      "allowedMemberTypes": ["User"],
+      "description": "Use standard agent features",
+      "displayName": "Agent user",
+      "isEnabled": true,
+      "value": "Agent.User"
+    }
+  ]
 }
 ```
 
-The `assignmentRequired` property ensures that only principals explicitly assigned an app role can access the agent identity blueprint, enforcing least privilege and preventing accidental access.
+This is role configuration on two separate objects, not permission inheritance or a downstream API grant. Don't create a blueprint principal for a single-instance agent.
+
+The service-principal definition supports `User` for users and groups. Don't add `Application` to this request: roles assignable to client applications must be defined on an application object. This single-instance procedure covers inbound user access, not application-only callers. See the [appRole resource reference](/graph/api/resources/approle).
+
+### Fleet access
+
+For a fleet, use the blueprint declaration without the single-instance service-principal update. Include `User` in `allowedMemberTypes` for users or groups and `Application` for client applications. For the application-level procedure, see [Add app roles to an application](~/identity-platform/howto-add-app-roles-in-apps.md). Use the blueprint principal, not a child Agent ID, as the resource for inbound assignments.
 
-## Assign app roles to control access
+## Verify the role on the resource principal
 
-App roles are granted through app role assignments. They link a principal (user, group, or agent identity) to a specific app role on the target agent identity. If an agent identity fails to access an application after configuration, verify that an `appRoleAssignment` is created for the agent identity using the APIs shown in the following example.
+Before requiring or assigning a role, read back the blueprint with `GET https://graph.microsoft.com/beta/applications/<blueprint-object-id>?$select=appRoles` and the agent API principal with `GET https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/servicePrincipals/<agent-api-service-principal-object-id>?$select=appRoles`. Use an authorized management client, not the agent's runtime token.
 
-### Assign an app role to a user
+Confirm that the principal's `appRoles` contains the role's exact `id` and `value`, that `isEnabled` is `true`, and that `allowedMemberTypes` includes the intended assignee type.
 
-The following example uses the Grant an `appRoleAssignment` to a user API to assign an app role to a user.
+If an assignment returns `Permission being assigned was not found on application`, check the role definition on the resource principal and the assignment's `resourceId` and `appRoleId`. For a single-instance agent, complete the direct definition above if you defined the role only on the blueprint. Don't create a blueprint principal, substitute another resource, or remove the API's role check. Continue only after the intended principal exposes the role.
+
+## Require an app role assignment
+
+Set `appRoleAssignmentRequired` on the agent API service principal. When the property is `true`, Microsoft Entra ID issues an access token for the agent API only to assigned users and applications.
 
 ```http
-POST https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/users/<user-id>/appRoleAssignments
-Authorization: Bearer <token with AppRoleAssignment.ReadWrite.All>
+PATCH https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/servicePrincipals/<agent-api-service-principal-object-id>
 Content-Type: application/json
+Authorization: Bearer <access-token>
 
 {
-  "principalId": "<user-id>",
-  "resourceId": "<agent-identity-blueprint-principal-id>",
-  "appRoleId": "<app-role-id>"
+  "appRoleAssignmentRequired": true
 }
 ```
 
-### Assign an app role to an agent identity
+For more information, see the [Microsoft Graph update API reference](/graph/api/serviceprincipal-update).
 
-The following example uses the Grant an `appRoleAssignment` to a service principal API to assign an app role to an agent identity.
+## Assign an app role
+
+Assign the app role to a user on the agent API service principal:
 
 ```http
-POST https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/servicePrincipals/<agent-identity-id>/appRoleAssignments
-Authorization: Bearer <token with AppRoleAssignment.ReadWrite.All>
+POST https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/users/<user-object-id>/appRoleAssignments
 Content-Type: application/json
+Authorization: Bearer <access-token>
 
 {
-  "principalId": "<agent-identity-id>",
-  "resourceId": "<agent-identity-blueprint-principal-id>",
+  "principalId": "<user-object-id>",
+  "resourceId": "<agent-api-service-principal-object-id>",
   "appRoleId": "<app-role-id>"
 }
 ```
 
-## Verify role assignment
+Use the GUID saved when you defined `Agent.User` as `<app-role-id>`. For a group, create the assignment through the group's app role assignments. For a fleet role that allows `Application`, create a client application's assignment through that client's service principal. In every case, use the agent API service principal's object ID as `resourceId`.
+
+## Enforce app roles in the agent API
+
+When an assigned user or application gets an access token for the agent API, Microsoft Entra ID includes the assigned app role values in the token's `roles` claim. The agent API checks that claim before it allows the requested operation.
+
+After [configuring authentication and token validation](aspnet-core-authenticate-users.md), add an authorization policy that requires the app role:
+
+In `Program.cs`, merge the policy registration into `builder.Services.AddAuthorization` before `builder.Build()`. Place the endpoint mapping after the authentication and authorization middleware and before `app.Run()`; the two parts of this fragment aren't adjacent in a complete application.
+
+```csharp
+builder.Services.AddAuthorization(options =>
+{
+    options.AddPolicy(
+        "AgentUser",
+        policy => policy.RequireRole("Agent.User"));
+});
+
+app.MapPost("/tasks", () => Results.Accepted())
+    .RequireAuthorization("AgentUser");
+```
 
-To verify your role assignment, be sure to take the following actions:
+`AddAuthorization` registers the ASP.NET Core authorization services. `RequireRole` checks the authenticated identity for the `Agent.User` role. Microsoft.Identity.Web recognizes Microsoft Entra app roles in the access token's `roles` claim.
 
-- List `appRoleAssignments` for the user or agent identity.
-- Check the roles claim in the token after sign-in.
+Call `UseAuthentication` before `UseAuthorization` in the middleware pipeline, as shown in the authentication article. Request a new access token after changing an assignment. When troubleshooting, verify the assignment on the agent API service principal and the token's `roles` claim.
 
-If roles claims are missing from tokens, verify that the assignment exists with the correct appRoleId, then request a new token. Regularly audit these assignments using Microsoft Graph or the Microsoft Entra admin center to ensure they remain appropriate and remove any unnecessary access.
+With a new token for the agent API and the assigned `Agent.User` role, the sample `POST /tasks` returns `202 Accepted`. Without a token, expect `401`; an otherwise valid token without that role is rejected with `403` if the tenant issues it. When assignment is required, Microsoft Entra ID might reject sign-in or token issuance before the request reaches your API.

-- [Microsoft Entra roles and permissions for agent identities](authorization-agent-id.md#microsoft-entra-roles-allowed-for-agents)
-- [conditional access for enhanced security controls](../identity/conditional-access/overview.md)

 # Plan your agent identity architecture
 
-Before you integrate your AI agent with Microsoft Entra Agent ID, you need to make a series of design decisions. This guide walks you through each decision in order:
+Use this guide when you're designing identity boundaries for a platform or several separately managed agents. Its tutorials include the required identity setup; this planning guide isn't a prerequisite.
 
-1. **Which identity type** your agent needs.
-1. **Which operation pattern** your agent uses, including how it acquires tokens and what context it acts in.
-1. **How many blueprints** your system requires.
-1. **How many agent identities** to create per blueprint.
+The guide helps you choose the identity type, operation pattern, and blueprint structure that match your access and lifecycle requirements.
 
-Work through these decisions in order, because earlier choices shape later ones. Some single-agent deployments might only need the first two steps. For examples of how these decisions map to real-world agent architectures, see [Agent ID design patterns](concept-agent-id-design-patterns.md).

+- **How many agent identities** to create per blueprint.
+- **Which instance mode** matches that identity relationship.
+
+Earlier choices shape later ones. The selected tutorial sets the instance mode during provisioning; it isn't a separate operating mode your users need to choose. For architecture examples, see [Agent ID design patterns](concept-agent-id-design-patterns.md).

+### Use an Agent ID for the agent's runtime identity

Microsoft Entra doesn't govern it as an agent, and labeling it an "agent identity" doesn't make it one.

-For more information about blueprints, see [Agent identity blueprints](identity-platform/agent-blueprint.md).
+For more information about blueprints, see [Agent identity blueprints](agent-blueprint.md).
 
 ## Step 4: Decide how many agent identities per blueprint
 
@@ -133,8 +140,16 @@ The following factors are *not* reasons to add more agent identities:
 
 Multi-agent architectures where multiple agent identities are appropriate can include sequential pipelines with distinct agent roles and concurrent orchestrations with specialized domain workers. For more information, see [AI agent orchestration patterns](/azure/architecture/ai-ml/guide/ai-agent-design-patterns).
 
+## Step 5: Choose the instance mode
+
+Choose the blueprint's mode before creating it. Single-instance mode represents one Agent ID per tenant, with the same OAuth client ID as the blueprint and no blueprint principal. Multi-instance mode supports separate child Agent IDs with distinct client IDs.
+
+Registered public-client agents must use single-instance mode. Confidential agents can also use it when one identity is appropriate. If the blueprint needs to provision identities with independent permissions or lifecycles, use multi-instance mode.
+
+Having only one child identity doesn't make an existing multi-instance blueprint single-instance. The setting is fixed at creation. For details, see [Blueprint instance modes](agent-blueprint.md#instance-modes-preview) and [Create a single-instance agent identity](create-single-instance-agent.md).

@@ -1,128 +1,133 @@

+title: Secure a web API with Microsoft Entra ID
+description: Configure a web API to validate Agent ID access tokens and authorize requests from agents and users.
 titleSuffix: Microsoft Entra Agent ID
-description: Learn how to validate Microsoft Entra Agent ID tokens in a downstream API by checking the signature, issuer, audience, and agent identity marker claim.
 ms.topic: how-to
-ms.date: 04/28/2026
-ms.custom: msecd-doc-authoring-1012
+ms.date: 11/05/2026
 ai-usage: ai-assisted
+ms.reviewer: dastrock
 
-#customer intent: As an API developer, I want to validate Microsoft Entra Agent ID tokens in my downstream API so that I can verify that requests come from authenticated agents with the correct identity.
-
+#customer-intent: As an API developer, I want to validate Agent ID tokens so that only authorized agents and users can call my API.
 ---
 
-# Validate agent identity tokens in a downstream API
+# Secure a web API with Microsoft Entra ID
+
+A downstream API must validate every access token before it trusts the Agent ID, user, or permissions represented by the token. Use a supported authentication middleware or token-validation library instead of parsing tokens in application code.
+
+This article covers Microsoft identity platform v2.0 access tokens.
+
+The API registration must expose the delegated scope or application role that each endpoint requires, and the calling client or agent must have the corresponding grant. For an assembled local delegated test, follow [Call a custom API as a user](aspnet-core-call-custom-api-as-user.md). For app-only caller setup and consent, follow [Call a custom API as an agent](call-api-custom.md).
 
-When an AI agent calls your API through the Microsoft Entra ID Auth SDK (sidecar), the request includes a `Bearer` token. Your API validates this token to confirm the request comes from an authenticated agent with the correct permissions. If validation fails, your API returns HTTP 401 with a reason.
+## Configure token validation
 
-This article explains the validation checks and shows how to configure and run a sample weather API that validates agent identity tokens end-to-end.
+Configure the API with:
 
-## Prerequisites
+- The Microsoft Entra tenant or accepted issuer set.
+- The API's Application ID URI or client ID as the expected audience.
+- Microsoft identity platform signing-key discovery.
+- The delegated scopes or application roles required by each operation.
 
-- **Docker Desktop** (macOS / Windows) or **Docker Engine** (Linux).
-- A **Microsoft Entra tenant** with an agent identity blueprint and an agent identity. For setup steps, see [Create an agent blueprint](create-blueprint.md) and [Create and delete agent identities](create-delete-agent-identities.md).
-- An agent identity token for testing. You can get one from the [sidecar local development sample](sidecar-local-development.md) or from the scripts in the [Microsoft Entra Agent ID samples repository](https://github.com/microsoft/entra-agentid-samples).
+For ASP.NET Core, use Microsoft.Identity.Web. For other frameworks, use a Microsoft-supported JWT validation library.
 
-## Token validation checks
+For complete registration and framework guidance, see [Configure protected web API apps](/entra/identity-platform/scenario-protected-web-api-app-configuration).
 
-Your downstream API should perform four checks on every incoming agent identity token:
+## Configure an ASP.NET Core API
 
-| Check | What it verifies | Details |
-|---|---|---|
-| **Signature** | The token isn't tampered with. | Verify the RS256 signature against the JSON Web Key Set (JWKS) at `https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant>/discovery/v2.0/keys`. |
-| **Issuer** | Microsoft Entra ID issued the token. | The `iss` claim matches `https://sts.windows.net/<tenant>/` or `https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant>/v2.0`. |
-| **Audience** | The token is intended for your API. | The `aud` claim matches your API's expected audience value. |
-| **Agent identity marker** | The token was issued to an agent, not a regular app. | The `xms_par_app_azp` claim is present in agent identity tokens and absent in standard app-only tokens. This claim identifies the blueprint that created the agent. |
+Install Microsoft.Identity.Web:
 
-When all four checks pass, your API can trust and process the request.
+```dotnetcli
+dotnet add package Microsoft.Identity.Web
+```
 
-## How the sample weather API works
+Configure the tenant and API registration:
 
-The [Microsoft Entra Agent ID samples repository](https://github.com/microsoft/entra-agentid-samples) includes a sample weather API that demonstrates these validation checks. The sample API is a minimal Flask app that acts as the downstream API your agent calls. It validates incoming agent identity tokens and returns real weather data from [Open-Meteo](https://open-meteo.com).
+```json
+{
+  "AzureAd": {
+    "Instance": "https://login.microsoftonline.com/",
+    "TenantId": "<tenant-id>",
+    "ClientId": "<downstream-api-client-id>"
+  }
+}
+```
 
-Both the [local development (Ollama)](sidecar-local-development.md) and AWS (Bedrock) sidecar samples call the same weather API container. The sample consists of three files:
+Register token validation and protect delegated and app-only endpoints:
 
-- **`app.py`:** Flask app with route handlers, token validation logic, and Open-Meteo client.
-- **`Dockerfile`:** Uses `python:3.13-slim` as the base image. Runs `gunicorn app:app` on port 8080.
-- **`requirements.txt`:** Dependencies: `flask`, `pyjwt[crypto]`, `cryptography`, `requests`, `gunicorn`.
+```csharp
+using Microsoft.Identity.Web;
+using Microsoft.Identity.Web.Resource;
 
-The API exposes two endpoints:
+var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);
 
-- **`GET /weather?city=<name>`:** Validates the `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header and returns weather data for the specified city.
-- **`GET /healthz`:** Returns a health status without requiring token validation.
+builder.Services.AddMicrosoftIdentityWebApiAuthentication(
+    builder.Configuration);
 
-The following diagram shows how tokens flow from the agent through the sidecar to the weather API. The agent never contacts Microsoft Entra ID directly. Instead, the sidecar acquires a token (TR) on behalf of the agent identity, and the agent passes that token to the weather API in the `Authorization: Bearer` header.
+builder.Services.AddAuthorization(options =>
+{
+    options.AddPolicy(
+        "AgentApplication",
+        policy => policy.RequireRole("Agent.Access"));
+});
 
-:::image type="content" source="media/how-to-validate-agent-tokens-downstream-api/agent-token-flow-to-downstream-api.png" alt-text="Diagram showing the agent caller sending a Bearer token to the weather API, which verifies the token and calls Open-Meteo." lightbox="media/how-to-validate-agent-tokens-downstream-api/agent-token-flow-to-downstream-api.png":::
+var app = builder.Build();
 
-The agent identity token, TR, is issued by Microsoft Entra ID through the sidecar. It contains the claims your API validates, including the `xms_par_app_azp` agent identity marker. For a detailed breakdown of all tokens in the flow, see [Run the sidecar for local development](sidecar-local-development.md#understand-the-token-flow).
+app.UseAuthentication();
+app.UseAuthorization();
 
-Token validation libraries differ across ecosystems (Python, Node.js, .NET). This sample uses PyJWT with the `cryptography` backend for RS256 signature verification. When you build your own downstream API, choose the equivalent JWT validation library for your technology stack.
+app.MapGet("/data-for-user", (HttpContext context) =>
+{
+    context.VerifyUserHasAnyAcceptedScope("access_as_user");
+    return Results.Ok();
+})
+.RequireAuthorization();
 
-## Configure the sample weather API
+app.MapGet("/data-for-agent", () => Results.Ok())
+    .RequireAuthorization("AgentApplication");
 
-The sample weather API accepts the following environment variables:
+app.Run();
+```
 
-| Variable | Required | Default | Purpose |
-|---|---|---|---|
-| `TENANT_ID` | Yes | — | Your Microsoft Entra tenant ID, used to build the JWKS URL and verify the issuer claim. |
-| `EXPECTED_AUDIENCE` | No | `https://graph.microsoft.com` | The expected `aud` claim value. Defaults to Microsoft Graph so that the same agent tokens work for local testing. |
-| `PORT` | No | `8080` | The HTTP port the API listens on. |
+Replace `access_as_user` with the delegated scope exposed by the API. Replace `Agent.Access` with the application role assigned to the Agent ID.
 
-## Run the sample weather API
+`AddMicrosoftIdentityWebApiAuthentication` validates the token signature, issuer, audience, and lifetime. `VerifyUserHasAnyAcceptedScope` enforces the delegated `scp` claim. `RequireRole` enforces the application permission in the `roles` claim.
 
-To run the weather API as a standalone container and test token validation:
+For more complete authorization patterns, see [Verify scopes and app roles in a protected web API](/entra/identity-platform/scenario-protected-web-api-verification-scope-app-roles).
 
-1. Clone the repository and navigate to the weather API directory:
+Test each endpoint with a token issued for **this downstream API**, not the agent's inbound token. With the required scope or role, the sample returns `200 OK`. Without a token or with the wrong audience, expect `401`. With an otherwise valid token for this API that lacks the required scope or role, expect rejection. Use the linked walkthroughs for token acquisition; don't return or log tokens to inspect them.
 
-    ```bash
-    git clone https://github.com/microsoft/entra-agentid-samples.git
-    cd entra-agentid-samples/sidecar/weather-api
-    ```
+## Validate the token
 
-1. Build and run the container:
+Reject the request unless all of these checks succeed:
 
-    ```bash
-    docker build -t weather-api:local .
-    docker run --rm -p 8080:8080 \
-      -e TENANT_ID=<your-tenant-id> \
-      -e EXPECTED_AUDIENCE=https://graph.microsoft.com \
-      weather-api:local
-    ```
+1. **Signature:** The token is signed by a trusted Microsoft Entra signing key.
+1. **Issuer:** The `iss` claim matches an issuer accepted by the API.
+1. **Audience:** The `aud` claim identifies this API.
+1. **Lifetime:** The token is within its valid time window.
+1. **Tenant:** The `tid` claim is allowed by the API's tenant policy.
+1. **Client:** The authorized-party claim identifies an allowed client or blueprint where the API restricts callers.
+1. **Agent identity:** Agent-specific claims, including the Agent ID relationship claims expected by the scenario, are present and valid.
+1. **Permission:** Delegated requests contain the required `scp` value; app-only requests contain the required `roles` value.
 
-1. Send a request with an agent identity token:
+Don't authorize a request based only on the presence of an Agent ID claim. Apply the same issuer, audience, lifetime, and permission checks used for other Microsoft Entra access tokens.
 
-    ```bash
-    curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
-         "http://localhost:8080/weather?city=Dallas"
-    ```
+## Distinguish access types
 
-The API returns a JSON response that includes both the weather data and the token validation results:
+| Access type | User context | Permission claim | API authorization |
+| --- | --- | --- | --- |
+| Agent acting as itself | None | `roles` | Verify the required application role and Agent ID. |
+| Agent acting for a signed-in user | Signed-in user | `scp` | Verify the scope, user authorization, and Agent ID. |
+| Agent acting as its user account | Agent's user account | `scp` | Verify the scope, account authorization, and Agent ID relationship. |
 
-```json
-{
-  "city": "Dallas",
-  "temperature": 61,
-  "temperature_unit": "F",
-  "condition": "Overcast",
-  "humidity": 93,
-  "wind_speed": 8,
-  "is_agent_identity": true,
-  "agent_app_id": "<agent-app-id from xms_par_app_azp>",
-  "validated_by": "Agent Identity Token",
-  "data_source": "Open-Meteo API (Real-time)"
-}
-```
+## Return authorization errors
 
-The `is_agent_identity`, `agent_app_id`, and `validated_by` fields confirm token validation:
+- Return `401 Unauthorized` when the token is missing or invalid.
+- Return `403 Forbidden` when the token is valid but lacks the required permission or resource access.
 
-- **`is_agent_identity`:** Set to `true` when the `xms_par_app_azp` claim is present, which confirms the token was issued to an agent identity rather than a standard app registration.
-- **`agent_app_id`:** The value of the `xms_par_app_azp` claim, which identifies the blueprint application that created the agent identity.
-- **`validated_by`:** The validation method applied to the token. Displays `Agent Identity Token` when the agent marker claim is present.
+Don't include tokens or sensitive claim values in logs.
 
 ## Related content
 
-- [Token claims reference](agent-token-claims.md)
-- [Authentication with Auth SDK (sidecar)](authentication-with-auth-sdk-sidecar.md)
-- [Run the sidecar for local development](sidecar-local-development.md)
-- [Microsoft Entra Agent ID samples repository](https://github.com/microsoft/entra-agentid-samples)
+- [Configure protected web API apps](/entra/identity-platform/scenario-protected-web-api-app-configuration)
+- [Verify scopes and app roles in a protected web API](/entra/identity-platform/scenario-protected-web-api-verification-scope-app-roles)
+- [Agent identity token claims](agent-token-claims.md)
+- [Microsoft identity platform access tokens](/entra/identity-platform/access-tokens)

 Deleting agent identity objects isn't supported in the Microsoft Entra admin center. Use Microsoft Graph API or Microsoft Entra PowerShell to delete blueprints and agent identities.
 
-You can delete the agent identity blueprint and blueprint principal separately. Deleting the app registration also deletes the principal. Deleting only the principal leaves the app registration in place.
+The blueprint application and blueprint principal are separate directory objects with separate delete endpoints. Use the endpoint for the object you intend to delete, then check the other object and related agent identities independently.
 
 > [!NOTE]
-> Standard deletion is always soft deletion. Objects are moved to the recycle bin, but not immediately removed. Permanent deletion happens automatically after 30 days, or you can force it using the standard hard-delete process described in [Deleting and recovering applications FAQ](../identity/enterprise-apps/delete-recover-faq.yml).

The [agentIdentity delete API](/graph/api/agentidentity-delete?view=graph-rest-beta&preserve-view=true) documents the same recovery period for an agent identity. The Graph delete API references don't specify whether deleting a blueprint application or principal also deletes child agent identities or associated agent user accounts.

 # Microsoft Entra Agent ID key concepts
 
-The Microsoft agent identity platform provides specialized identity constructs designed specifically for AI agents operating in enterprise environments. These identity constructs enable secure authentication and authorization patterns that differ from traditional user and application identities, addressing the unique requirements of autonomous AI systems.
+An agent identity lets an AI agent authenticate to APIs and other resources. Its agent identity blueprint holds authentication settings and credentials, while the agent identity receives access to resources. For example, an agent that reads a protected API needs a blueprint, an agent identity, and permission to call that API.
 
-This article explains the core concepts that form the foundation of agent identity management: agent identities, agent identity blueprints, and their supporting components. -The agent identity architecture follows a hierarchical model where agent identity blueprints serve as templates for creating multiple agent instances, each with distinct identities and capabilities. This approach enables centralized management while providing the flexibility needed for diverse AI agent deployment scenarios.
+An agent identity blueprint defines the configuration for one or more agent identities. In multi-instance mode, it provides a template for separate child identities. In single-instance mode, the blueprint and its one Agent ID share an OAuth client ID, with no blueprint principal.
