-# Acquire tokens and call downstream APIs with Microsoft Entra ID Auth SDK (sidecar)
+# Configure the Microsoft Entra ID Auth SDK sidecar
+
+The Microsoft Entra ID Auth SDK sidecar is a companion service that handles authentication and token acquisition for your agent. It lets your cloud agent call APIs as itself or on behalf of signed-in users.
 
-The Microsoft Entra ID Auth SDK (sidecar) is a containerized web service that handles token acquisition, validation, and downstream API calls for agents. This SDK communicates with your application through HTTP APIs, providing consistent integration patterns regardless of your technology stack. Instead of embedding identity logic directly in your application code, the Microsoft Entra ID Auth SDK (sidecar) manages token acquisition, validation, and API calls through standard HTTP requests.
+In this article, you configure the sidecar container, its blueprint credential, and downstream API access.
 
 ## Prerequisites
 
-Before you begin, ensure you have:
+- Completion of [Create an identity for your agent](create-single-instance-agent.md), including tenant enablement, administrator approvals, and the recorded client and object IDs.
+- A credential configured on the blueprint.
+- Permissions granted to the Agent ID for each downstream API.
+- A shared network namespace for the agent and sidecar, such as containers in the same pod.
+
+## Add the sidecar container
+
+Run the agent and sidecar in the same network namespace and call the sidecar through `localhost`. Production sidecar builds restrict callers to loopback; a private Docker bridge and a `sidecar` DNS name aren't sufficient. Containers in the same Kubernetes pod or Azure Container Apps app share this boundary. In Docker Compose, use `network_mode: "service:sidecar"` on the agent. Don't publish the sidecar port.
+
+Use the credential configuration for where you run the container:
+
+- **Local workstation:** Follow [Run the sidecar for local development](sidecar-local-development.md) for the sample container startup and development credential. Apply the network boundary above and the API profiles and override settings below.
+- **Azure host:** Use the following configuration after assigning the managed identity to the host and configuring its federated credential on the blueprint. It doesn't provide a workstation credential.
+
+The Docker Compose fragment illustrates the shared network layout and uses a user-assigned managed identity as the credential:
+
+Set `AzureAd:ClientCredentials:0:SourceType` to `SignedAssertionFromManagedIdentity` and `AzureAd:ClientCredentials:0:ManagedIdentityClientId` to the user-assigned managed identity's client ID. This is a different value from the shared agent client ID in `AzureAd:ClientId`. Container environment variables use `__` in place of `:` in these configuration paths.
+
+Record the tenant, blueprint, Agent ID, and API identifiers for your scenario in the [scenario identifier worksheet](key-concepts.md#record-the-identifiers-for-your-scenario) before configuring these values.
 
-- [Set up the Microsoft Entra ID Auth SDK (sidecar)](/entra/msidweb/agent-id-sdk/installation)
-- [An agent identity](./create-delete-agent-identities.md). Record the agent identity client ID.
-- [An agent identity blueprint](./create-blueprint.md). Record the agent identity blueprint client ID.
-- Necessary [permissions configured in Microsoft Entra ID](grant-agent-access-microsoft-365.md)
+```yml
+services:
+  sidecar:
+    image: mcr.microsoft.com/entra-sdk/auth-sidecar:1.1.3-azurelinux3.0-distroless
+    environment:
+      AzureAd__Instance: https://login.microsoftonline.com/
+      AzureAd__TenantId: <tenant-id>
+      AzureAd__ClientId: <agent-client-id>
+      AzureAd__ClientCredentials__0__SourceType: SignedAssertionFromManagedIdentity
+      AzureAd__ClientCredentials__0__ManagedIdentityClientId: <managed-identity-client-id>
+      ASPNETCORE_URLS: http://localhost:5000
 
-## Deploy your containerized service
+  agent:
+    image: <agent-image>
+    network_mode: "service:sidecar"
+    environment:
+      SIDECAR_URL: http://localhost:5000
+```
 
-Deploy the Microsoft Entra ID Auth SDK (sidecar) as a containerized service in your environment. Follow the instructions in the [Set up the Microsoft Entra ID Auth SDK (sidecar)](/entra/msidweb/agent-id-sdk/installation) guide to configure the service with your agent identity details.
+Replace `<agent-image>` with your agent's image. This example pins the Linux sidecar to `1.1.3-azurelinux3.0-distroless`. For Windows, use the matching Windows tag from [Auth SDK sidecar container image tags](https://mcr.microsoft.com/v2/entra-sdk/auth-sidecar/tags/list).
 
-## Configure your Microsoft Entra ID Auth SDK (sidecar) settings
+Use `SignedAssertionFilePath` instead when the container receives a workload identity token from its orchestrator. Use `ClientSecret` only for local development. Don't place the blueprint credential in the agent container.
 
-Follow these steps to configure your Microsoft Entra ID Auth SDK (sidecar) settings:
+For other credential sources, see [Microsoft.Identity.Web credential descriptions](https://aka.ms/ms-id-web/credential-description).
 
-[!INCLUDE [Dont use secrets](./includes/do-not-use-secrets.md)]
+## Configure a downstream API
 
-1. Set up the necessary components in Microsoft Entra ID. Ensure you register your application in the Microsoft Entra ID tenant.
+Give each downstream API a short name. Configure its base URL, scopes, and token type. For example, this profile requests app-only tokens for Microsoft Graph:
 
-1. Configure your client credentials. This credential can be a client secret, a certificate, or a managed identity that you're using as a federated identity credential. 
+```json
+{
+  "DownstreamApis": {
+    "graph-app": {
+      "BaseUrl": "https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/",
+      "Scopes": [
+        "https://graph.microsoft.com/.default"
+      ],
+      "RequestAppToken": true
+    }
+  }
+}
+```
 
-1. If you're calling a downstream API, ensure that the necessary permissions are granted. Calling a custom web API requires you to provide the API registration details in the SDK configuration.
+The name becomes the `{apiName}` route value. This example uses `graph-app`, so the agent requests `/AuthorizationHeaderUnauthenticated/graph-app`.

+The resource-specific articles provide the configuration for each API. To configure the container with environment variables, replace each `:` in the JSON path with `__`. For example:
 
-## Acquire tokens using the Microsoft Entra ID Auth SDK (sidecar)
+```yml
+environment:
+  DownstreamApis__graph-app__BaseUrl: https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/
+  DownstreamApis__graph-app__Scopes__0: https://graph.microsoft.com/.default
+  DownstreamApis__graph-app__RequestAppToken: "true"
+```
 
-These are the steps to acquire tokens using the Microsoft Entra ID Auth SDK (sidecar):
+## Keep identity overrides disabled
 
-1. Acquire token using the Microsoft Entra ID Auth SDK (sidecar). This varies based on whether the agent is operating autonomously or on behalf of a user. There are three scenarios to consider:
+Use the client ID recorded during setup directly. Don't pass `AgentIdentity`, `AgentUserId`, or `AgentUsername`: these select a different identity flow, not the cloud-agent setup in this article.
 
-    - Autonomous agents: Agents operating on their own behalf using service principals created for agents (autonomous).
-    - Autonomous agent's user account: Agents operating on their own behalf using user principals created specifically for agents (for instance agents having their own mailbox).
-    - Interactive agents: Agents operating on behalf of human users.
+Keep overrides disabled on the endpoints used by the agent:
 
-    Specify the downstream API by including its name in the request URL based on your Microsoft Entra ID Auth SDK (sidecar) configuration. +```json
+{
+  "Sidecar": {
+    "AllowOverrides": {
+      "GetAuthorizationHeader": false,
+      "GetAuthorizationHeaderUnauthenticated": false,
+      "CallDownstreamApi": false,
+      "CallDownstreamApiUnauthenticated": false
+    }
+  }

-    ```bash
-    GET /AuthorizationHeader/Graph?AgentIdentity=<agent-identity-client-id>
-    Authorization: Bearer eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGc...
-    ```

-1. To acquire token for an autonomous agent's user account, provide either the user object ID or User Principal Name but not both. This means providing either `AgentUsername` or `AgentUserId`. If the agent identity parameter is missing, the request fails with a validation error.

+ms.reviewer: dastrock
 ai-usage: ai-assisted
 
-#customer-intent: As a developer building or securing an MCP server, I want to implement OAuth 2.0 correctly with Microsoft Entra ID as the authorization server so that MCP clients and agents can obtain and present valid access tokens for my server.
+#customer-intent: As an MCP server developer, I want to protect my server with Microsoft Entra ID so that only authorized clients, users, and agents can call it.
 ---
 
-# Secure a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server with Microsoft Entra ID
+# Secure a Model Context Protocol server with Microsoft Entra ID
 
-The [Model Context Protocol (MCP)](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) lets AI agents and other clients call tools and data sources that you expose from an MCP server. Because an MCP server can act on behalf of a user or an autonomous agent, you should protect it like any other API: require an OAuth 2.0 access token on every request, and validate that token before you run a tool.
+An MCP server is an OAuth 2.0 protected resource. Register the server as an API in Microsoft Entra ID, publish protected-resource metadata, and validate each access token before processing an MCP request.
 
-This article explains how to configure Microsoft Entra ID as the authorization server for your MCP server, register the server so that MCP clients can request tokens for it, and connect an MCP client by using [Microsoft Entra Agent ID](what-is-microsoft-entra-agent-id.md).
-
-> [!IMPORTANT]
-> Don't write your own token-validation logic from scratch. Token validation bugs can silently expose your MCP server to unauthorized callers. Use a well-tested authentication library or middleware for your platform, and follow the source-of-truth guidance linked in [Validate access tokens in your MCP server](#validate-access-tokens-in-your-mcp-server).
+This guidance supports Microsoft identity platform v2.0 access tokens only.
 
 ## Prerequisites
 
-- A **Microsoft Entra tenant** where you can register applications. To register apps, you need at least the [Application Developer](/entra/identity/role-based-access-control/permissions-reference#application-developer) role.
-- An **MCP server** that you host at an HTTPS URL, for example `https://mcp.contoso.com`.
-- Familiarity with the [MCP authorization specification](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/basic/authorization), which builds on OAuth 2.1, [Resource Indicators for OAuth 2.0 (RFC 8707)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8707), and [OAuth 2.0 Protected Resource Metadata (RFC 9728)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9728).
-
-## How MCP authorization works with Microsoft Entra ID
-
-In the MCP authorization model:
-
-- Your **MCP server** is an OAuth 2.0 *protected resource*.
-- **Microsoft Entra ID** is the *authorization server* that issues access tokens.
-- The **MCP client**, such as an agent, is the *client* that requests a token and presents it to your server.
-
-The MCP specification requires the client to identify the protected resource it wants a token for by sending the `resource` parameter (from RFC 8707) in its token request. The value of `resource` is the canonical URL of your MCP server. Microsoft Entra ID compares that `resource` value against the **Application ID URI** (also called the identifier URI) configured on your MCP server's app registration. If they match, Microsoft Entra ID issues a token whose audience (`aud`) claim is your MCP server. If they don't match, the token request fails.
-
-For this matching to work, your MCP server must accept **v2 access tokens**. See [Register your MCP server in Microsoft Entra ID](#register-your-mcp-server-in-microsoft-entra-id) for the exact steps to configure the access token version.
-
-The end-to-end flow looks like this:
-
-1. The MCP client discovers your server's authorization requirements. When an unauthenticated request arrives, your server returns `HTTP 401` with a `WWW-Authenticate` header that points to your [protected resource metadata (RFC 9728)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9728), which in turn identifies Microsoft Entra ID as the authorization server.
-1. The MCP client requests an access token from Microsoft Entra ID, sending `resource=<your MCP server URL>`.
-1. Microsoft Entra ID validates the request, matches `resource` to your app registration's Application ID URI, and issues a v2 access token scoped to your server.
-1. The MCP client calls your MCP server with the token in the `Authorization: Bearer` header.
-1. Your MCP server validates the token and, if it's valid, runs the requested tool.
-
-## Register your MCP server in Microsoft Entra ID
-
-Register your MCP server as an application so that Microsoft Entra ID can issue tokens for it. 
-
-If your MCP server is served by an an existing web service or REST API that is already secured by Entra - you may re-use its existing app registration and its OAuth scopes.
-
-The order of the following steps matters: you must enable v2 access tokens *before* you can set an HTTPS Application ID URI that matches your server URL.
+- A Microsoft Entra tenant.
+- An HTTPS endpoint for the MCP server.
+- Permission to create an app registration and grant consent.
+- An MCP client that supports OAuth protected-resource metadata.
 
-### Step 1: Create the app registration
+## Register the MCP server
 
-1. Sign in to the [Microsoft Entra admin center](https://entra.microsoft.com).
-1. Browse to **Entra ID** > **App registrations** > **New registration**.
-1. Enter a name for your MCP server, such as `Contoso MCP server`, and select **Register**.
+1. Register an application for the MCP server.
+1. Set an Application ID URI that uniquely identifies the server.
+1. Expose the delegated scopes required by MCP clients.
+1. Define application roles only if the server supports app-only access.
+1. Record the tenant ID, application client ID, and Application ID URI.
 
-### Step 2: Set the access token version to v2
+Grant only the permissions required by the tools and resources that the server exposes.
 
-This is the step that most people miss. Your app registration must request v2 access tokens by setting `requestedAccessTokenVersion` to `2` in the [Microsoft Graph app manifest](/entra/identity-platform/reference-microsoft-graph-app-manifest#api-attribute).
+## Publish protected-resource metadata
 
-1. In your app registration, select **Manifest**.
-1. In the `api` object, set `requestedAccessTokenVersion` to `2`:
+Publish a metadata document at `<server-url>/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource`. MCP clients that support OAuth protected-resource discovery fetch this document to find the authorization server and supported scopes before requesting a token.
 
-    ```json
-    "api": {
-        "requestedAccessTokenVersion": 2
-    }
-    ```
-
-1. Select **Save**.
-
-> [!NOTE]
-> If you skip this step and leave the app on v1 access tokens, you can't set an HTTPS Application ID URI that matches your MCP server's URL, and MCP clients that send `resource=<your MCP server URL>` receive an error. See [FAQ and troubleshooting](#faq-and-troubleshooting).
-
-### Step 3: Set the Application ID URI to your MCP server URL
-
-After the app issues v2 access tokens, set the Application ID URI to the exact canonical URL of your MCP server. This value is what MCP clients send in the `resource` parameter.
-
-1. In your app registration, select **Expose an API**.
-1. Next to **Application ID URI**, select **Add** (or **Edit**), and enter your MCP server's URL, for example `https://mcp.contoso.com`.
-1. Select **Save**.
-
-Alternatively, set `identifierUris` directly in the manifest. The `identifierUris` property is a list, so if your MCP server is reachable at more than one URL, add every URL that clients might use. A client typically sends the URL it connected to as its `resource` value, and Microsoft Entra ID only issues a token when that value exactly matches one of the registered Application ID URIs.
-
-```json
-"identifierUris": [
-    "https://mcp.contoso.com",
-    "https://mcp.contoso.com/mcp",
-    "https://contoso-mcp.azurewebsites.net"
-]
-```
-
-### Step 4: Define scopes
-
-Delegated scopes let an MCP client that acts on behalf of a signed-in user request only the level of access it needs. If your MCP server serves interactive clients, define at least one OAuth scope so that clients can request a token for your server and users or administrators can consent to it.
-
-1. In your app registration, select **Expose an API**.
-1. Select **Add a scope**.
-1. Enter a scope name that reflects an operation your server exposes, such as `tool.read` or `tool.execute`.
-1. Choose who can consent (**Admins only**, or **Admins and users**), enter the consent display names and descriptions, set the state to **Enabled**, and select **Add scope**.
-
-An MCP client then requests the fully qualified scope, which combines your Application ID URI and the scope name — for example, `https://mcp.contoso.com/tool.execute`.
-
-Define as many OAuth scopes as needed to provide granular access to your MCP server.
-
-### Step 5 (Optional): Define app roles
-
-In addition to acting on behalf of users, MCP clients can also authenticate as an agent identity. To request an access token as an agent identity, the MCP client sends an OAuth client credentials grant request and uses a scope value such as `scope=https://mcp.contoso.com/.default`.
-
-Entra **app roles** can be used to limit the access an MCP client has against your MCP server. You assign app roles to the MCP client's agent identity. Assigned roles appear in the `roles` claim of the access token, and your server checks that claim before it runs a tool.
-
-1. In your app registration, select **App roles** > **Create app role**.
-1. Enter a display name and a value such as `Tools.Execute.All`, set **Allowed member types** to **Applications**, and enable the role.
-1. Assign the role to the agent identity (or other client application) that calls your server.
-
-For more information, see [Add app roles and receive them in the token](/entra/identity-platform/howto-add-app-roles-in-apps).
-
-## Publish protected resource metadata
-
-MCP clients discover how to authenticate to your server by reading its [OAuth 2.0 Protected Resource Metadata (PRM)](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9728) document. The MCP authorization specification requires every HTTP MCP server to serve a PRM document and to reference it from the `WWW-Authenticate` header of its `401` responses. The document tells clients which authorization server to use (Microsoft Entra ID) and which resource identifier to request a token for.
-
-Serve the document as JSON from the well-known path derived from your server's URL, for example `https://mcp.contoso.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource`. For a server secured by Microsoft Entra ID, it should look like this:
+The following example shows a minimal document for a Microsoft Entra-backed MCP server:
 
 ```json
 {
   "resource": "https://mcp.contoso.com",
   "authorization_servers": [
-    "https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant-id>/v2.0"
+    "https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant-id>/oauth21/2026-08"
   ],
   "scopes_supported": [
-    "tools.read",
-    "tools.execute"
+    "mcp.access"
   ],
-  "bearer_methods_supported": ["header"]
+  "bearer_methods_supported": [
+    "header"
+  ]
 }
 ```
 
-Set the fields as follows:
-
-- **`resource`** — the canonical URL of your MCP server. This value must be identical to the Application ID URI you registered in [Step 3](#step-3-set-the-application-id-uri-to-your-mcp-server-url) and to the `resource` parameter that clients send. If your server exposes multiple URLs, each PRM document describes one specific URL, and clients request metadata for the URL they connected to.
-- **`authorization_servers`** — the Microsoft Entra ID issuer for your tenant, `https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant-id>/v2.0`. Clients perform authorization server metadata discovery against this issuer (for example, at `https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant-id>/v2.0/.well-known/openid-configuration`) to find Entra's authorization and token endpoints. Use your tenant ID or a verified domain; use `organizations` or `common` in place of the tenant ID only for multitenant servers.
-- **`scopes_supported`** — optional. List the delegated scopes you defined in [Step 4](#step-4-define-scopes). Clients use these to decide what to request when the `WWW-Authenticate` challenge doesn't specify a `scope`.
-- **`bearer_methods_supported`** — set to `["header"]` because your server expects the token in the `Authorization: Bearer` request header.
+- **`resource`** — The Application ID URI registered for the MCP server. This value must match the `aud` claim the server expects in incoming tokens.
+- **`authorization_servers`** — The Microsoft Entra authorization server URL, `https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant>/oauth21/2026-08`. Use your tenant ID for a server that accepts users from a single tenant, or `common` for a server that accepts users from any organization. Clients append `/.well-known/openid-configuration` to this URL to discover the authorization and token endpoints.
+- **`scopes_supported`** — The delegated scopes exposed by the MCP server. List only the scopes clients need to call the server.
+- **`bearer_methods_supported`** — Set to `["header"]` to indicate that clients must send the token in the `Authorization` request header.
 
-> [!IMPORTANT]
-> The `authorization_servers` value must be the **v2.0** issuer (`.../v2.0`), which matches the `iss` claim of the v2 access tokens your server accepts (see [Step 2](#step-2-set-the-access-token-version-to-v2)). The v1 issuer (`https://sts.windows.net/<tenant-id>/`) doesn't line up with the v2.0 authorization server metadata that clients discover.
+For the full metadata format and discovery behavior, see the [MCP authorization specification](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/basic/authorization).
 
-On an unauthenticated request, return a `401` response whose `WWW-Authenticate` header points to this document. Optionally include a `scope` parameter to tell the client which scopes the current operation requires:
+## Validate access tokens
 
-```http
-HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
-WWW-Authenticate: Bearer resource_metadata="https://mcp.contoso.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource", scope="tools.execute"
-```
+Require an access token on protected MCP requests. Validate the token's signature, issuer, audience, lifetime, tenant, client, and permissions.
 
-If you use an official MCP SDK or Azure App Service authentication, the platform can generate and serve this document and the `401` challenge for you. See [Validate access tokens in your MCP server](#validate-access-tokens-in-your-mcp-server).
+Use the MCP server's Application ID URI or client ID as the expected audience, according to its registration. Enforce delegated scopes from `scp` and application permissions from `roles`.
 
-## Validate access tokens in your MCP server
+For the complete validation checklist, see [Validate Agent ID tokens in a downstream API](how-to-validate-agent-tokens-downstream-api.md).
 
-On every request, your MCP server must validate the access token before it runs a tool. At a minimum, verify the token's **signature**, **issuer** (`iss`), **tenant ID** (`tid`), **audience** (`aud`, which must equal the application ID of your MCP server), and expiry. Then check that the **subject** (`sub` or `oid`) of the token is authorized for the requested operation using the **role** (`roles`) claim or another authorization check. For delegated access tokens, also be sure to check the **scope** (`scp`) claim to confirm the caller / actor is authorized for the requested operation.
+## Configure token validation in ASP.NET Core
 
-To avoid introducing a security vulnerability, don't implement these checks by hand. Use the guidance and libraries in the following source-of-truth articles:
+Install Microsoft.Identity.Web:
 
-- [Protected web API: overview](/entra/identity-platform/scenario-protected-web-api-overview) and [Protected web API: code configuration](/entra/identity-platform/scenario-protected-web-api-app-configuration) — the canonical pattern for protecting an API with Microsoft Entra ID, including recommended middleware such as Microsoft.Identity.Web.
-- [Secure access tokens](/entra/identity-platform/access-tokens) and [Validate tokens](/entra/identity-platform/access-tokens#validate-tokens) — how to validate signature, issuer, and audience correctly.
-- [Secure applications and APIs by validating claims](/entra/identity-platform/claims-validation) — how to authorize requests by validating the claims in a token, beyond signature and audience checks.
-- [Validate agent identity tokens in a downstream API](how-to-validate-agent-tokens-downstream-api.md) — a worked example for Microsoft Entra Agent ID tokens, including how to detect that a caller is an agent identity.
-
-If you host your MCP server on **Azure App Service**, you can offload authentication to the platform's built-in authentication (Easy Auth) instead of validating tokens in your app code. For step-by-step guidance, see [Secure MCP servers with Microsoft Entra authentication on Azure App Service](/azure/app-service/configure-authentication-mcp-server-vscode).
+```dotnetcli
+dotnet add package Microsoft.Identity.Web
+```
 
-## Connect an MCP client using Microsoft Entra Agent ID
+Configure the tenant and MCP server registration:
 
-When the MCP client is an AI agent, use [Microsoft Entra Agent ID](what-is-microsoft-entra-agent-id.md) so the agent authenticates with its own identity instead of an embedded secret. The agent acquires a token for your MCP server and presents it on each call.
+```json
+{
+  "AzureAd": {
+    "Instance": "https://login.microsoftonline.com/",
+    "TenantId": "<tenant-id>",
+    "ClientId": "<mcp-server-client-id>"
+  }
+}
+```
 
-1. Set up the agent's identity. See [Create and delete agent identities](create-delete-agent-identities.md) and [Authentication protocols in agents](agent-oauth-protocols.md).
-1. Grant the agent access to your MCP server, either by consenting to a delegated scope that you defined in [Step 4](#step-4-define-scopes) or by assigning an app role that you defined in [Step 5](#step-5-optional-define-app-roles).
-1. Have the agent acquire a token for your MCP server. The client sends `resource=<your MCP server URL>` (per the MCP specification) and requests the appropriate OAuth scope.
-1. The agent calls your MCP server with the token in the `Authorization: Bearer` header. Your server validates it as described in [Validate access tokens in your MCP server](#validate-access-tokens-in-your-mcp-server).
+Register token validation and define a policy for the MCP delegated scope or application role:
 
-For a broader view of how agents call protected resources, see [Configure third-party agents with Agent ID](configure-third-party-agents.md) and [Call custom APIs from an agent](call-api-custom.md).
+```csharp
+using Microsoft.Identity.Web;
 
-## FAQ and troubleshooting
+var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);
 
-### Should my MCP server use v1 or v2 access tokens?
+builder.Services.AddMicrosoftIdentityWebApiAuthentication(
+    builder.Configuration);
 
-Use **v2 access tokens**. Set `requestedAccessTokenVersion` to `2` on your MCP server's app registration, as described in [Step 2](#step-2-set-the-access-token-version-to-v2). MCP authorization relies on matching the client's `resource` parameter to an HTTPS Application ID URI, and that configuration requires v2 tokens.
+builder.Services.AddAuthorization(options =>
+{
+    options.AddPolicy("McpAccess", policy =>
+    {
+        policy.RequireAuthenticatedUser();
+        policy.RequireAssertion(context =>
+            context.User.IsInRole("Mcp.Access")
+            || context.User.FindAll("scp").Any(claim =>
+                claim.Value
+                    .Split(' ', StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries)
+                    .Contains("mcp.access", StringComparer.Ordinal)));
+    });
+});
+
+var app = builder.Build();
+
+app.UseAuthentication();
+app.UseAuthorization();
+
+app.MapPost("/mcp", () => Results.Ok())
+    .RequireAuthorization("McpAccess");
+
+app.Run();
+```
 
-### I get error AADSTS9010010 when a client requests a token for my MCP server
+Replace `mcp.access` with the delegated scope exposed by the MCP server. Replace `Mcp.Access` with its application role. Apply the `McpAccess` policy to the endpoint mapped by the MCP server framework rather than adding a second `/mcp` route.
 
-`AADSTS9010010` means the **Application ID URI configured on your app registration doesn't exactly match the value of the `resource` parameter** in the client's OAuth request. To fix it:
+The `Results.Ok()` handler is an authorization placeholder, not an MCP implementation. After applying the policy to your framework's endpoint, verify that an authorized client can perform the intended MCP tool or resource operation. Also test a missing token and a valid token without the required permission; an HTTP success from the placeholder alone doesn't verify MCP interoperability.
 
-1. **Check for a trailing slash or other exact-match difference.** The `resource` value the client sends must match the Application ID URI character for character, including the scheme (`https://`), casing of the host, and path. A trailing slash is a common culprit: because an Application ID URI can't end with a slash, a client that sends `resource=https://mcp.contoso.com/` never matches the registered `https://mcp.contoso.com`. Remove the trailing slash (and any other difference) so the client's `resource` value and the Application ID URI are identical.
-1. **Confirm your app uses v2 access tokens.** If `requestedAccessTokenVersion` isn't set to `2`, you can't register an HTTPS Application ID URI that matches your MCP server URL, so the `resource` value can never match. Complete [Step 2](#step-2-set-the-access-token-version-to-v2), then re-add the Application ID URI in [Step 3](#step-3-set-the-application-id-uri-to-your-mcp-server-url).
-1. **Make sure the requested scope belongs to the same app registration as the `resource`.** This error also occurs when the client sends a scope that's defined on a *different* app registration than the one referenced by the `resource` parameter. Microsoft Entra ID resolves the `resource` and the scope to the same resource app; if they point at different app registrations, the request fails. Confirm that every scope the client requests is exposed by the app registration whose Application ID URI you send in `resource`, and remove any scope that belongs to another app.
+The authentication middleware returns `401 Unauthorized` for a missing or invalid token. The authorization policy returns `403 Forbidden` when a valid token lacks both the required delegated scope and application role.
 
-### What if I can't use v2 access tokens?
+For complete framework and authorization guidance, see [Configure protected web API apps](/entra/identity-platform/scenario-protected-web-api-app-configuration) and [Verify scopes and app roles in a protected web API](/entra/identity-platform/scenario-protected-web-api-verification-scope-app-roles).
 
-Some MCP servers reuse an existing app registration that already issues v1 access tokens to other clients, and can't switch to v2 tokens without breaking those clients. In that case, you can keep v1 tokens and instead make the `aud` claim deterministic by configuring the [`aud` optional claim](/entra/identity-platform/optional-claims-reference#v10-specific-optional-claims-set) with the `use_guid` [additional property](/entra/identity-platform/optional-claims-reference#additionalproperties-of-optional-claims).
+## Connect a client
 
-By default, the `aud` claim in a v1 access token is nondeterministic — Microsoft Entra ID can emit any of the app's Application ID URIs (with or without a trailing slash) or the resource's client ID. Setting `use_guid` forces `aud` to *always* be the resource's client ID in GUID format. Because the audience is no longer tied to a specific Application ID URI, Microsoft Entra ID relaxes the Application ID URI restrictions for the app, so you can add your MCP server's HTTPS URL as an Application ID URI ([Step 3](#step-3-set-the-application-id-uri-to-your-mcp-server-url)) even though the app still issues v1 tokens. Clients can then send `resource=<your MCP server URL>` and receive a token.
+The client discovers the protected-resource metadata, signs in or authenticates through Microsoft Entra ID, requests a token for the MCP server, and sends the token in the request's `Authorization` header.
 
-Add the optional claim to your app registration's manifest:
+Use one of these client identity models:
 
-```json
-"optionalClaims": {
-    "accessToken": [
-        {
-            "name": "aud",
-            "additionalProperties": ["use_guid"]
-        }
-    ]
-}
-```
+- A registered Agent ID.
+- A local public-client Agent ID using authorization code flow with PKCE.
+- A [Client ID Metadata Document](client-id-metadata-documents.md) URL when preregistration isn't practical.
 
-With `use_guid` set, the token's `aud` claim is your resource's **client ID** (a GUID), not your MCP server URL. Configure your MCP server (or the middleware or MCP SDK that validates tokens) to expect that client-ID GUID as the audience. Whenever you can move to v2 tokens, prefer that approach ([Step 2](#step-2-set-the-access-token-version-to-v2)), because the v2 `aud` claim is consistently the resource's client ID and aligns with the authorization server metadata that MCP clients discover.
+The MCP server doesn't need different token-validation logic for CIMD clients. Microsoft Entra ID still issues the access token, and the server validates it against the same issuer and audience policy.

Use the [Docker Compose configuration](microsoft-entra-sdk-for-agent-identities.md#add-the-sidecar-container), not separate containers communicating through a `sidecar` DNS name. The agent (`llm-agent-dev`) receives the query and decides to call the `get_weather` tool. -1. This type is the default for this sample. -- **`SignedAssertionFromManagedIdentity`:** Deployed on Azure. Zero secrets, recommended for production. -- **`KeyVault`:** Certificate from Azure Key Vault. -- **`StoreWithThumbprint`:** Certificate from local machine store. - -## Set up OBO sign-in (optional) - -To test the on-behalf-of flow, create the SPA app and configure OBO consent. +Add language customizations under **Company Branding** or for a specific user flow under **User flows**. For supported languages and instructions, see [Customize the language of the authentication experience](how-to-customize-languages-customers.md).
 
 ## Microsoft Graph APIs
 
 You can also manage company branding and configure all assets programmatically. 
 - For the default branding, use the [organizationalBranding resource type](/graph/api/resources/organizationalbranding) and its associated methods.
-- To customize branding based on locale, using the [organizationalBrandingLocalization resource type](/graph/api/resources/organizationalbrandinglocalization) resource type and its associated methods.

-title: Custom authentication extensions
-description: Learn how to use custom authentication extensions in Microsoft Entra External ID. Integrate with external systems, add custom logic to authentication flows, and enhance user experiences.
+title: Custom Authentication Extensions
+description: Use Microsoft Entra External ID custom authentication extensions to customize attribute collection, email passcode delivery, and token issuance.
 ms.topic: concept-article
-ms.date: 04/10/2025
-ms.custom: it-pro
+ms.date: 11/13/2026
+ms.custom: it-pro, msecd-doc-authoring-1030
+ai-usage: ai-assisted
+#customer intent: As a developer or IT administrator, I want to understand custom authentication extension events so that I can customize attribute collection, email passcode delivery, and token issuance.
+---
+# Custom authentication extensions in Microsoft Entra External ID
 
-#Customer intent: As a dev, devops, or it admin, I want to know 
+Custom authentication extensions add business logic at specific events in Microsoft Entra External ID sign-up and sign-in flows. An extension listens for an event and calls a REST API endpoint where you define a workflow action. For example, an extension can validate submitted sign-up attributes or add claims from an external system before token issuance.
 
----
-# Extend authentication flows with your own business logic
+[!INCLUDE [authentication-approaches](../includes/applies-to-authentication-approaches.md)]
 
-[!INCLUDE [applies-to-external-only](../includes/applies-to-external-only.md)]
+## Event coverage by authentication approach
 
-Microsoft Entra External ID user flows are designed for flexibility. Within a sign-up and sign-in user flow, there are built-in authentication events. You can also add custom authentication extensions at specific points within the authentication flow. A custom authentication extension is essentially an event listener that, when activated, makes an HTTP call to a REST API endpoint where you define a workflow action. For example, you could add an [attribute collection](#attribute-collection-start-and-submit-events) workflow to validate the attributes a user enters during sign-up, or you could use a [custom claims provider](#token-issuance-start-event) to add external user data to the token before the token is issued.
+[!INCLUDE [native-authentication-public-preview](../includes/native-authentication-public-preview.md)]
 
-> [!NOTE]
-> Token-issuance extensions (the **OnTokenIssuanceStart** event) apply to both browser-delegated and native authentication, because the extension runs server-side just before the token is issued. Attribute-collection extensions (the **OnAttributeCollectionStart** and **OnAttributeCollectionSubmit** events) apply only to **browser-delegated authentication**, because they fire on the Microsoft-hosted attribute collection page. For help choosing an approach, see [Choose an authentication approach](concept-choose-authentication-approach.md).
+Tenant, application, and user-flow configuration define the extension and the event listener. The event also needs a supported execution point in the selected integration. Sharing tenant policies doesn't imply that every authentication approach executes every event.
 
-There are two components you need to configure: a custom authentication extension and a REST API. The custom authentication extension specifies your REST API endpoint, when the REST API should be called, and the credentials to call the REST API. You can create custom authentication extensions at the following points in the authentication flow:
+Confirm event availability for your approach and API or SDK version in the [custom authentication extension event comparison](concept-supported-features-customers.md#custom-authentication-extension-applicability).
 
-- During sign-up, before or after attribute collection:
-  - The **OnAttributeCollectionStart** event occurs at the beginning of the attribute collection step, before the attribute collection page renders.
-  - The **OnAttributeCollectionSubmit** event occurs after the user enters and submits attributes.
-- Upon token issuance using the **OnTokenIssuanceStart** event, which triggers just before a token is issued to the application.
+Use the event's documented inputs and responses. Support for the four documented events doesn't establish password-migration hooks, password-update synchronization, or arbitrary context propagation. For architectural guidance, see [Choose an authentication approach](concept-choose-authentication-approach.md).
 
-:::image type="content" source="media/concept-custom-extensions/authentication-flow-events-inline.png" alt-text="Diagram showing extensibility points in the authentication flow." lightbox="media/concept-custom-extensions/authentication-flow-events-expanded.png" border="false":::
+Configure two components: a custom authentication extension and a REST API. The extension specifies the REST API endpoint, when to call it, and the credentials for the call. You can create extensions at the following points in the authentication flow:
 
-If you have a custom authentication extension configured at one of these points, Microsoft Entra ID makes a call to the REST API you define. The request to the REST API contains information about the event, the user profile, authentication request data, and other context information. In turn, the REST API performs the workflow actions.
+- During sign-up, before or after attribute collection.
+- When sending an email one-time passcode through a configured email provider.
+- Upon token issuance, before the configured claims are added to the application's token.
 
-This article provides an overview of custom authentication extensions in Microsoft Entra External ID.
+:::image type="content" source="media/concept-custom-extensions/authentication-flow-events-inline.png" alt-text="Diagram of attribute collection and token issuance extension points." lightbox="media/concept-custom-extensions/authentication-flow-events-expanded.png" border="false":::
+
+When an applicable event runs, Microsoft Entra ID calls your REST API with the event's defined payload. The REST API returns one of the actions supported by that event. Use the event's documented payload to determine which application context is available.
 
 ## Attribute collection start and submit events
 
-You can use custom authentication extensions to add workflows to attribute collection in your self-service sign-up user flows. For example, you can prefill attribute fields with custom values, validate a user's entries, and modify attributes, and display errors. Two events are enabled:
+Use these events with Microsoft-hosted authentication to prefill fields, validate entries, modify attributes, or block self-service sign-up. `OnAttributeCollectionStart` and `OnAttributeCollectionSubmit` aren't supported for Embedded native authentication or Bring Your Own UX. Ordinary attribute collection through the Native Authentication API doesn't enable these extension events; follow the [attribute collection contract](~/identity-platform/concept-native-authentication-user-attributes.md) instead.
 
-- **OnAttributeCollectionStart** - The OnAttributeCollectionStart event occurs at the beginning of the attribute collection process before the attribute collection page renders. This event can be used for scenarios like preventing the user from signing up based on their domain or adding attributes to be collected. The following scenarios are configurable for the OnAttributeCollectionStart event:
+- **OnAttributeCollectionStart** - This event runs before attribute collection. It can prefill attributes or block sign-up, for example based on the customer's email domain. The supported actions are:
 
-  - **continueWithDefaultBehavior** - Render the attribute collection page as usual.
+  - **continueWithDefaultBehavior** - Continue with the configured attribute collection.
   - **setPreFillValues** - Prefill attributes in the sign-up form.
   - **showBlockPage** - Show an error message and block the user from signing up.
 
@@ -51,9 +54,17 @@ To configure the attribute collection start and submit events, you create a cust
 
 For details, see [Add attribute collection custom extensions to your user flow](~/identity-platform/custom-extension-attribute-collection.md?context=/entra/external-id/customers/context/customers-context).
 
+For attribute collection without these extension events, see [Native authentication user attributes](../../identity-platform/concept-native-authentication-user-attributes.md).
+
+## Email one-time passcode send event
+
+The `OnOtpSend` event lets a configured provider send email one-time passcodes. It doesn't register an MFA method or make email eligible as both the first and second factor. The service's current transaction still determines the required verification.
+
+For setup, see [Configure a custom email provider](~/identity-platform/custom-extension-email-otp-get-started.md).
+
 ## Token issuance start event
 
-The token issuance start event is triggered once a user completes all of their authentication challenges and a security token is about to be issued.
+The token issuance start event occurs after a user completes all authentication challenges, just before a security token is issued.
 
 When users authenticate to your application with Microsoft Entra ID, a security token is returned to your application. The security token contains claims that are statements about the user, such as name, unique identifier, or application roles. Beyond the default set of claims that are contained in the security token, you can define your own custom claims from external systems using a REST API you develop.

modifiedFiles.patch: diff --git a/docs/external-id/customers/concept-multifactor-authentication-customers.md b/docs/external-id/customers/concept-multifactor-authentication-customers.md index 465a1fb97c4..78de046034a 100644 --- a/docs/external-id/customers/concept-multifactor-authentication-customers.md +++ b/docs/external-id/customers/concept-multifactor-authentication-customers.md @@ -1,34 +1,45 @@ --- -title: MFA in external tenants -description: Learn about using MFA to secure apps in your external tenant and enabling email one-time passcodes (EOTP), SMS, time-based one-time passwords (TOTP), or passkeys (FIDO2) for verification. +title: Multifactor Authentication +description: Explore multifactor authentication in Microsoft Entra External ID, including methods, policies, and availability for each authentication approach. ms.topic: concept-article -ms.date: 11/06/2026 -ms.custom: it-pro, references_regions +ms.date: 11/13/2026 +ms.custom: it-pro, references_regions, msecd-doc-authoring-1030 ai-usage: ai-assisted -#Customer intent: As a dev, devops, or it admin, I want to learn about ways to secure apps in my external tenant by adding multifactor authentication and enabling SMS, email one-time passcodes, TOTP, and passkeys. +#customer intent: As an application developer or IT administrator, I want to understand multifactor authentication methods and policies so that I can secure apps in my external tenant. --- -# Multifactor authentication in external tenants +# Multifactor authentication in Microsoft Entra External ID external tenants -[!INCLUDE [applies-to-external-only](../includes/applies-to-external-only.md)] +Multifactor authentication (MFA) in Microsoft Entra External ID helps protect your applications by requiring additional verification during sign-up or sign-in. -Multifactor authentication (MFA) adds a layer of security to your applications by requiring users to provide a second method for verifying their identity during sign-up or sign-in. External tenants support the following methods for authentication as a second factor: +[!INCLUDE [authentication-approaches](../includes/applies-to-authentication-approaches.md)] -- Email one-time passcode -- SMS-based authentication, available as an add-on ([see details](#sms-based-authentication)). -- Time-based one-time password (TOTP) from Microsoft Authenticator or a supported third-party authenticator app ([see details](#time-based-one-time-password-totp)). -- Passkey (FIDO2). Passkeys are a phishing-resistant authentication method that can satisfy MFA in a single gesture and also enable passwordless sign-in ([see details](#passkey-fido2)). +The following methods can be configured in an external tenant. Runtime method and registration support depends on the selected authentication approach and API/SDK version. -Enforcing MFA enhances your organization's security by adding an extra layer of verification, making it more difficult for unauthorized users to gain access. +- Email one-time passcode (OTP). +- [SMS-based authentication](#sms-based-authentication), available as an add-on. +- [Time-based one-time password (TOTP)](#time-based-one-time-password-totp) from Microsoft Authenticator or a supported third-party authenticator app. +- [Passkey (FIDO2)](#passkey-fido2), a phishing-resistant method that can satisfy MFA in a single gesture and also enable passwordless sign-in. -> [!NOTE] -> MFA is supported for both browser-delegated and native authentication. With browser-delegated authentication, the MFA challenge is handled on the Microsoft-hosted sign-in page. With native authentication, your app surfaces the MFA prompt inline using the MSAL SDK; if the app doesn't advertise the `mfa_required` capability, the native authentication API initiates a [web fallback](/entra/identity-platform/concept-native-authentication-web-fallback) to complete the challenge. For more information about choosing an approach, see [Choose an authentication approach](concept-choose-authentication-approach.md). +## Authentication approach applicability + +Configure MFA policies and methods in your external tenant. Confirm method coverage and registration requirements in the [MFA support matrix](concept-supported-features-customers.md#multifactor-authentication-behavior). For policy enforcement and browser fallback support, see the [integration and policy comparison](concept-supported-features-customers.md#integration-policy-and-sessions-by-approach). + +[!INCLUDE [native-authentication-public-preview](../includes/native-authentication-public-preview.md)] + +With the Native Authentication API, inline registration uses the returned `enroll` and `activate` operations and can satisfy the policy without a separate MFA challenge. Complete required verification after sign-up or password reset before requesting tokens or completing a BYO UX browser flow. + +A separate native-app browser sign-in restarts authentication. It isn't an escape-to-web-and-resume mechanism for an active native or BYO UX transaction. See the [Native authentication overview](../../identity-platform/concept-native-authentication.md) and [Bring Your Own UX guidance](concept-choose-authentication-approach.md#when-to-use-bring-your-own-ux). + +For architectural guidance, see [Choose an authentication approach](concept-choose-authentication-approach.md). -## Creating an MFA policy + -In an external tenant, you can use Microsoft Entra Conditional Access to create a policy that prompts users for MFA when they sign up or sign in to your app. You create this policy in the Microsoft Entra admin center under Conditional Access in the Protection section. You can specify which users and groups the policy apply to, including all users and excluding any emergency access or break-glass accounts. +## Create an MFA policy + +In an external tenant, you can use Microsoft Entra Conditional Access to create a policy that prompts users for MFA when they sign up or sign in to your app. You create this policy in the Microsoft Entra admin center under Conditional Access in the Protection section. You can specify which users and groups the policy applies to, including all users and excluding any emergency access or break-glass accounts. In the policy, you define the applications that require MFA. You can apply the policy to all cloud apps or select specific apps, while excluding any applications that don't require MFA. Then you configure the policy to grant access only if users complete the MFA requirement. @@ -36,15 +47,21 @@ For details, see [how to create a Conditional Access policy in an external tenan ### Step-up MFA with Conditional Access authentication context -Multifactor authentication (MFA) with authentication context lets you apply stronger security only when users access sensitive data or perform critical actions. You don’t need to enforce MFA for the entire app. +MFA with authentication context lets you require additional verification when users access sensitive data or perform critical actions, rather than for the entire app. With Microsoft Entra [Conditional Access authentication context](/entra/identity-platform/developer-guide-conditional-access-authentication-context), developers can add step-up authentication, such as MFA, inside their apps. Use this for scenarios like high-value transactions or viewing personal information. -This approach supports Zero Trust principles. It ensures least privilege access and reduces user friction. Users get a secure and seamless experience. +This approach supports Zero Trust principles and least-privilege access while reducing user friction. + +This later-operation step-up capability applies to Microsoft-hosted authentication and BYO UX, not Embedded native authentication. Satisfying claims and MFA requirements established at the start of a native authorization transaction is different from requesting step-up for a later operation. + + -## Enabling MFA methods +## Enable MFA methods When you select identity provider options in your user flows, you define the first-factor authentication methods for sign-up and sign-in. Second-factor verification methods for MFA are configured in the Microsoft Entra admin center under **Entra ID** > **Authentication methods**. -Depending on which option you choose as the first factor, different second-factor verification methods are available for [multifactor authentication (MFA)](how-to-multifactor-authentication-customers.md). +With Microsoft-hosted authentication, the first-factor choice determines which second-factor methods are available for [multifactor authentication (MFA)](how-to-multifactor-authentication-customers.md). For the Native Authentication API and BYO UX, the supported second factors are email and SMS, subject to the same restriction against reusing email OTP as both factors. - **Email with password or username with password**: For these first-factor methods, you can enable email one-time passcode, SMS, TOTP, passkey (FIDO2), or a combination as second-factor verification methods for MFA. - **External identity providers**: You can enable email one-time passcode, SMS, TOTP, or a combination as second-factor verification methods for MFA. See [Service limits and restrictions](reference-service-limits.md). -- CAPTCHA for SMS MFA helps prevent automated attacks by distinguishing human users from automated bots. If a risky user is detected, we block the user from signing in or ask the user to complete a CAPTCHA before sending an SMS verification code. +- CAPTCHA for SMS MFA helps prevent automated attacks by distinguishing human users from bots. Use this guide to prioritize controls and integrations that help protect your customer-facing applications. -External-facing identity systems support a wide range of customer experiences. Understanding these threats helps explain why a clear, layered security approach is essential. Microsoft Entra External ID provides foundational capabilities you can build on. -We have a single, unified [Microsoft Authentication Library (MSAL)](~/identity-platform/msal-overview.md) where the same application code works for workforce and customer scenarios. In three steps, you can sign up or sign in a user:
+For Microsoft-hosted authentication, use the [Microsoft Authentication Library (MSAL)](~/identity-platform/msal-overview.md) to integrate a browser-based sign-in flow. The following steps summarize that integration:
 
-1. Configure MSAL to use to your tenant and application
-1. Create a sign-in function that calls MSAL to start the web-based sign in flow
-1. Create a response handler which can extract customer information from the returned token
+1. Configure MSAL for your tenant and application.
+1. Create a sign-in function that calls MSAL to start the browser-based sign-in flow.
+1. Create a response handler that reads user information from the authentication result.
 
-You can see example code for each of these steps in our [sample applications](samples-ciam-all.md).
+For example code, see the [sample applications](samples-ciam-all.md).
 
 ### Can I build a fully custom authentication sign-in experience?
 
-Yes. Microsoft Entra External ID supports two authentication approaches: **browser-delegated authentication**, which redirects users to a Microsoft-hosted sign-in page, and **native authentication**, which lets you build the sign-in UI directly into your app. Native authentication gives you full control over the sign-in experience for mobile and single-page applications but requires more development effort and shared security responsibility. To compare both approaches and decide which is right for your app, see [Choose an authentication approach](concept-choose-authentication-approach.md).
+For customer apps in external tenants, yes. You can customize Microsoft-hosted pages, use **Embedded native authentication** to add sign-in screens to your app, or use **Bring Your Own UX (BYO UX)** within a browser flow. To compare the options, see [Choose an authentication approach](concept-choose-authentication-approach.md).

 ### What integrations does External ID support for developers?
 
-External ID supports server-side integrations with external systems via [custom authentication extensions](~/identity-platform/custom-extension-overview.md). This capability allows developers to implement their own logic and invoke it via real-time API calls during sign-in/up flows.
+External ID supports server-side integrations through [custom authentication extensions](~/identity-platform/custom-extension-overview.md). Use these extensions to invoke your business logic through real-time API calls during sign-up and sign-in flows.

 # Enable self-service password reset
 
-[!INCLUDE [applies-to-external-only](../includes/applies-to-external-only.md)]
-
 Self-service password reset (SSPR) in Microsoft Entra External ID gives customers the ability to change or reset their password, with no administrator or help desk involvement. If a customer's account is locked or they forget their password, they can follow prompts to unblock themselves and get back to work.
 
+[!INCLUDE [authentication-approaches](../includes/applies-to-authentication-approaches.md)]
+
 ## How the password reset process works
 
-Self-service password reset (SSPR) supports two authentication methods: email one-time passcode (Email OTP) and SMS. When SSPR is enabled, users who forget their password can verify their identity using either Email OTP or SMS. With one-time passcode authentication, a passcode is sent by email or SMS. After entering the passcode, the user is prompted to create a new password.
+For Microsoft-hosted authentication, self-service password reset (SSPR) supports email one-time passcode (Email OTP) and SMS. When SSPR is enabled, users who forget their password can verify their identity using a configured recovery method. After entering the passcode, the user is prompted to create a new password. Native Authentication API and SDK recovery availability must be checked separately in the comparison.
 
-The process works as follows:
+The Microsoft-hosted password-reset process works as follows:
 
 1. From the app, the user selects **Sign in**.
 1. On the sign-in page, they enter their email address and choose **Next**.

 # Add multifactor authentication (MFA) to an app
 
-[!INCLUDE [applies-to-external-only](../includes/applies-to-external-only.md)]
+Multifactor authentication (MFA) adds a layer of security to your applications by requiring users to provide a second method for verifying their identity during sign-up or sign-in.
 
-Multifactor authentication (MFA) adds a layer of security to your applications by requiring users to provide a second method for verifying their identity during sign-up or sign-in. External tenants support the following methods for authentication as a second factor:
+[!INCLUDE [authentication-approaches](../includes/applies-to-authentication-approaches.md)]
+
+The following user experiences describe Microsoft-hosted authentication. Tenant policy configuration is shared, but runtime method and enrollment support varies by integration.
 
 - **Email one-time passcode**: After the user signs in with their email and password, they are prompted for a passcode that is sent to their email. To allow the use of email one-time passcodes for MFA, set your local account authentication method to *Email with password*. If you choose *Email with one-time passcode*, customers who use this method for primary sign-in won't be able to use it for MFA secondary verification.
-- **SMS-based authentication**: While SMS isn't an option for first factor authentication, it's available as a second factor for MFA. Users who sign in with email and password, email and one-time passcode, or social identities like Google, Facebook or Apple, are prompted for second verification using SMS. Our SMS MFA includes automatic fraud checks. If we suspect fraud, we'll ask the user to complete a CAPTCHA to confirm they're not a robot before sending the SMS code for verification. It also provides safeguards against [telephony fraud](how-to-region-code-opt-in.md). SMS is an add-on feature. Your tenant must be [linked](../external-identities-pricing.md#link-an-external-tenant-to-a-subscription) to an active, valid subscription. [Learn more](concept-multifactor-authentication-customers.md#sms-based-authentication)
+- **SMS-based authentication**: While SMS isn't an option for first factor authentication, it's available as a second factor for MFA. Users who sign in with email and password, email and one-time passcode, or social identities like Google, Facebook or Apple, are prompted for second verification using SMS. SMS MFA includes automatic fraud checks. On Microsoft-hosted pages, these checks can require a CAPTCHA before an SMS code is sent. It also provides safeguards against [telephony fraud](how-to-region-code-opt-in.md). SMS is an add-on feature. Your tenant must be [linked](../external-identities-pricing.md#link-an-external-tenant-to-a-subscription) to an active, valid subscription. [Learn more](concept-multifactor-authentication-customers.md#sms-based-authentication)
 - **Time-based one-time password (TOTP)**: Users register Microsoft Authenticator or a supported third-party authenticator app. When MFA is required, they enter the temporary verification code from the app.
 - **Passkey (FIDO2)**: Passkeys provide phishing-resistant, passwordless authentication that satisfies MFA in a single gesture (face, fingerprint, PIN, or security key). Users can also use a passkey as a primary, passwordless sign-in method. For setup, see [Sign in with passkeys](how-to-sign-in-with-passkey.md).

+A user flow defines how customers sign up and sign in to your application and which attributes you collect.
 
-> [!TIP]
-> User flows are created in the Microsoft Entra admin center the same way for both authentication approaches. The instructions in this article apply whether your app uses **browser-delegated authentication** (Microsoft-hosted sign-in pages) or **native authentication** (sign-in UI built into your app). -You can create a simple sign-up and sign-in experience for your customers by adding a user flow to your application. modifiedFiles.patch: diff --git a/docs/identity-platform/concept-native-authentication-web-fallback.md b/docs/identity-platform/concept-native-authentication-web-fallback.md index fdf3e530d3d..2cf7691ce71 100644 --- a/docs/identity-platform/concept-native-authentication-web-fallback.md +++ b/docs/identity-platform/concept-native-authentication-web-fallback.md @@ -1,52 +1,73 @@ --- -title: Native authentication web fallback -description: Learn how you can use web fallback to improve the resilience of your customer apps that use native authentication. -manager: dougeby -ms.service: identity-platform -ms.subservice: external +title: Embedded native authentication web fallback overview +description: Understand unsupported native interactions, separate browser sign-in, and the boundaries between restarting and resuming authentication. ms.topic: concept-article -ms.date: 08/08/2025 - -#Customer intent: As a developer, devops, I want to learn more native authentication web fallback, so that I can enable it in my client apps. +ms.date: 11/13/2026 +ms.custom: msecd-doc-authoring-1030 +ai-usage: ai-assisted +#customer intent: As an application developer, I want to understand browser fallback so that my app can offer recovery when it can't complete a native interaction. --- -# Native authentication web fallback +# Embedded native authentication web fallback overview [!INCLUDE [applies-to-external-only](../external-id/includes/applies-to-external-only.md)] -Web fallback allows a client app that uses native authentication to use browser-delegated authentication as a fallback mechanism to improve resilience. This scenario happens when native authentication isn't sufficient to complete the authentication flow. For example, if the authorization server requires capabilities that the client can't provide. +[!INCLUDE [applies-to-authentication-native](../external-id/includes/applies-to-authentication-native.md)] + +An Embedded native authentication interaction can require behavior that your app can't complete natively. Browser fallback is a recovery path that starts a separate, configured browser sign-in. It doesn't resume the native transaction. + +[!INCLUDE [native-authentication-public-preview](~/external-id/includes/native-authentication-public-preview.md)] + + + +## Service-required and client-initiated fallback + +The API uses states, actions, and links to describe the next interaction. A client can present available actions or apply application flow logic to select an allowed operation. + +The Native Authentication API can return the following response: + +```json +{ + "state": "redirect" +} +``` + +This response can contain only `state`. It doesn't supply a continuation token or a browser handoff URL. Stop the native transaction instead of requiring `action`, `continuationToken`, or `_links` on this response. + +At the OAuth boundary, browser-required handling can instead use `invalid_grant` with `web_redirect_required`. Handle that OAuth error separately from native JSON states. + +A client can also reach a response it can't safely process: an unknown required action, a missing required field, an unsupported credential interaction, or malformed data. Offer a separately configured browser sign-in if your app has one, or show a clear failure without marking the user signed in. + +Unknown optional properties or links are different. Ignore those additions while processing the required fields; their presence alone doesn't require a switch to the browser. + +## Transaction and user-experience boundaries + +A separate browser sign-in restarts authentication; it doesn't preserve native progress. -All client apps that use native authentications needs to support web fallback. +Native continuation tokens belong to the active transaction and current operation. They aren't general-purpose browser sign-in tokens. Don't add passwords, one-time passcodes (OTPs), native continuation tokens, or security tokens to browser URLs. Let the configured authorization flow handle its registered redirect. Keep authorization codes and other credentials out of logs and telemetry. Use the configured interactive authorization flow, not an arbitrary URL supplied by untrusted content. -## Web fallback flow +The browser flow can have different interactions from the native flow. Don't mark the app signed in until its configured authentication integration reports success. If the user cancels or the browser flow fails, retain a clear signed-out or incomplete state. -This flow shows how web fallback can happen: - -- The client app collects initial information from the user and starts the authentication flow by making a request to Microsoft Entra. -- Microsoft Entra returns a success or error response. A success response indicates the client app can continue making requests Microsoft Entra. An error response can indicate the client can continue to prompt the user for more information and continue to make requests to Microsoft Entra. The error response can also indicate the client needs to use browser-delegated authentication. -- If the error response indicates the client needs to use browser-delegated authentication, the client continues the authentication flow in the browser. + + + -### Example scenario +## Browser integration -Let's look at an example when it's possible for Microsoft Entra to indicate that the client needs to use browser-delegated authentication: +Use a supported browser-delegated integration to open the browser and handle its registered redirect. The [mobile quickstart](quickstart-mobile-app-sign-in.md?pivots=external) and [single-page app quickstart](quickstart-single-page-app-sign-in.md?pivots=external) describe those integration paths. Keep browser completion, cancellation, and error handling separate from native transaction processing. -- In the Microsoft Entra admin center, an administrator configures an app to use email with password authentication method. -- This configuration means Microsoft Entra requires the client app to have the ability to collect an email (username) and password from user. The client app communicates this ability to Microsoft Entra by sending *password* challenge type. Learn more about challenge types in [Native authentication challenge types](concept-native-authentication-challenge-types.md) article. -- The client app should also validate the email by submitting a one-time passcode that the server sends to the user's email. The client app communicates this ability to Microsoft Entra by sending *oob* challenge type. Learn more about challenge types in [Native authentication challenge types](concept-native-authentication-challenge-types.md) article -- If the client app doesn't send both *oob* and *password* challenge types, Microsoft Entra interprets it as the client app's inability to fulfill the set requirement. In this case, Microsoft Entra returns an error that indicates the client needs to use browser-delegated authentication. +For an application configured with Bring Your Own UX (BYO UX), normal browser authorization uses the configured self-hosted page. A native `redirect` response isn't a URL or parameter for bypassing that configuration to Microsoft-hosted pages. Use the configured browser authorization flow rather than a constructed bypass URL. -## Support web fallback +If your app doesn't have a supported browser path, explain that the interaction can't be completed. Don't automatically replay credentials or switch the active transaction to V1. -If Microsoft Entra's response indicates that the client app needs to fall back to the browser-delegated authentication, we recommend you use a [Microsoft-built and supported authentication library](reference-v2-libraries.md). +## V1 fallback -Learn how to support web fallback in the following apps when you use native authentication: -- [Android apps](/entra/external-id/customers/tutorial-native-authentication-android-support-web-fallback). -- [iOS/macOS apps](/entra/external-id/customers/tutorial-native-authentication-ios-macos-support-web-fallback). -- [Single-page apps](tutorial-native-authentication-single-page-app-javascript-sdk-web-fallback.md). +V1 clients need to support web fallback. The client declares its supported interactions through challenge types. For example, an email-with-password user flow requires both `oob` and `password`; omitting either can cause the service to require browser authentication. See [V1 challenge types](reference-native-authentication-api-v1.md#v1-challenge-types-and-capabilities). +For existing SDK integrations, use the [SDK library references](reference-native-authentication-api-v1.md#sdk-references) for fallback interfaces. V1 fallback starts a separate browser sign-in, not a resumable native-to-browser continuation. ## Related content -- [Tutorial: Support web fallback in Android app](/entra/external-id/customers/tutorial-native-authentication-android-support-web-fallback) -- [Tutorial: Support web fallback in iOS/macOS app](/entra/external-id/customers/tutorial-native-authentication-ios-macos-support-web-fallback) -- [Tutorial: Support web fallback in SPA that uses native authentication JavaScript SDK](tutorial-native-authentication-single-page-app-javascript-sdk-web-fallback.md) \ No newline at end of file +- [Embedded native authentication flow](concept-native-authentication-flow.md). +- [The Native Authentication API reference](reference-native-authentication.md). +- [Migrate from Native Authentication API V1 to V2](how-to-migrate-native-authentication-v1-v2.md).
